#3202. Bread as a Sponge for Oil Is the Best Kitchen Hack I Learned All Year

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Oily pans, stews and sauces are no match for the bread sponge trick.

If you want to degrease a pan or the top layer of an oily sauce without ruining a sponge, a single slice of bread could be your new favorite cleaning sidekick.

While we have vastly improved how we dispose of most things, excess cooking grease still presents a problem. Down the sink? Not advisable. Neither is the dishwasher—even the garbage bin can become a gnarly affair.

Getting the bulk of the grease out of a pan after cooking a batch of bacon or burgers is a good first step, but that greasy pan will either take down a sponge or half a roll of paper towels. What if a humble slice of past-its-prime sandwich bread was the all-natural solution for greasy pans you’ve been looking for?

It’s cheap and easy, and you can toss the used-up bread into a compost bin or countertop food waste processor without disrupting its yuck-free operation.

So, is it ever OK to pour excess grease or used cooking oil down the sink? Even if you run the hot water tap at the same time? Short answer: no. Long answer? Here’s an expert for the “no.” “When grease cools, it solidifies, coating the interior of the pipe,” says Jacylyn Basilone, chief operating officer of Brooks Plumbing. Even if you’re running hot water, the grease will eventually cool further down the line and cause future problems. “Over time, the solidified grease in the pipes can catch debris, thus making a partial clog grow larger and larger,” she says, reducing the pipe’s circumference little by little if you do this repeatedly.

Unlike a clogged shower drain, which you can usually clear easily, “a normal sewer machine or ‘snake’ can’t alleviate this type of stoppage,” says Basilone. “While grease solidifies, it can’t be captured by the claw head. Grease removal is best remediated with a hydrojetter, which tends to be more expensive than the traditional drain-cleaning services.”

Bread is the real answer, and I can’t believe I haven’t been doing this all along. (*Hangs head in shame, fully guilty of relying on the obviously very sketchy hot water method.*)

Bread has always been a superb grease-mopping tool; we usually think of it in a culinary context rather than for waste removal. Just as you’d drag a crusty baguette or hunk of ciabatta across the drippings on your plate, bread is an excellent sponge for all manner of oil, whether or not it is appealing to consume. Using bread to soak up excess oil essentially turns liquid food waste into a solid, making disposal much easier.

If it’s not obvious, this is also a great way to use bread that might otherwise go to waste: the ends of the loaf you can’t bring yourself to eat, or bread that’s gone stale or is starting to show the first mold spores. If you’re going to discard the bread anyway, at least put it to good use.

The bread trick comes in handy in almost endless ways. If there’s a pool of oil, it’s the mop for the job. I initially tried it after cooking bacon. A single, small slice of bread was enough to absorb what was easily four to six ounces of liquid grease left in the pan. I dragged the slice around the pan like a mop, but even after letting it sit a few extra moments, it kept working and eventually soaked up all the liquid grease. (If you’re feeling indulgent and used a fresh bread slice for this purpose, the temptation to make pretty epic croutons here is quite strong — another upside.)

If your air fryer has space between the drawer and the basket, you can place the bread there to soak up grease while cooking. Even for oily, slow-cooked proteins like pork shoulder, you can press the bread onto the meat to soak up grease before serving.

Once the bread has absorbed the oil and needs discarding, responsible food-waste methods are much easier to manage. Depending on how much oil the bread has absorbed, you can safely put the soaked bread in the compost bin or countertop composter without risking a major oil spill and a mess to clean up later. Oil can slow decomposition, so composting large amounts isn’t recommended. Small amounts, such as a few tablespoons at a time, are safe.

Even if you have no other option but to throw it away — and if that is the case, please consider getting a small composting appliance — at the very least, you’re not involving an easily recyclable glass container.

For more home tips, learn this neat trick for reusing frying oil and learn the 10 worst things to pour down your drain.

You can more than triple the Edge's GPS battery life without sacrificing accuracy

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The new Fitbit Edge features onboard GPS, which is a very good thing for folks who enjoy outdoor workouts, and also just one of the many reasons it's one of the best fitness trackers you can buy.

Unlike the more entry-level Fitbit Air, you can accurately log location, distance, speed, pace, climb, and more with the Edge without needing to carry a paired smartphone.

There is one downside to the Fitbit Edge's onboard GPS though: it uses a lot of battery. Just to be clear, the wearable's overall battery life is pretty solid; I averaged about a week of use per charge while writing the Fitbit Edge review.

However, when using the Edge's onboard GPS for location tracking, it burns through roughly 12% battery per hour. This translates to just over eight hours of use before it's lights out.

Fortunately, there are a few ways to minimize battery drain without sacrificing location tracking insights. Both can be found in the Google Health app under Devices > Fitbit Edge > Device preferences > GPS settings.

Here you can switch location tracking from built-in to either dynamic — which uses both your smartphone and the onboard antenna — or smartphone-only.

The disadvantage of switching off the onboard GPS, of course, is that you now need to haul your smartphone along. But then again, if you're logging an eight-plus-hour workout, it may not be a bad idea to carry a means of communication just in case of emergencies.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Battery drain after one hour of workout tracking

More crucially, the non-onboard GPS options significantly reduce battery consumption in my testing. For example, switching to dynamic GPS increases battery life from around eight hours to closer to 25 hours for outdoor workouts.

But does turning off the onboard GPS negatively impact tracking accuracy? The Google Health app seems to suggest that it might, noting that the built-in option offers "high accuracy" while the dynamic one "automatically switches between devices to optimize battery and accuracy." Hmmm..

To find out if there's really a difference in tracking accuracy between the three GPS modes, I logged three 30-minute walking workouts using each one. As a control, I also logged the walks using my reliable Garmin Forerunner 170 Music, worn on the opposite wrist.

In my first test using only onboard GPS, the Fitbit Edge delivered impressively similar data to the control, including a step count total that's off by only one.

When using the Fitbit Edge's dynamic GPS mode, which switches between the onboard and smartphone-based antennas, the Edge once again logged data that falls remarkably well in line with the control across the board.

Finally, let's see how the Fitbit Edge performs in smartphone GPS-only mode.

With the exception of somewhat sluggish pace data, the Fitbit Edge's smartphone-only GPS tracking mode is also right on the money in terms of step count, distance, and climb data.

Ultimately, all three Fitbit Edge GPS modes delivered accurate-enough results that I'd confidently rely on any of them going forward, but is one definitively the best? That's going to truly come down to the user.

For example, I plan to set and leave the Edge's built-in tracking switched on unless a particularly long hike or multi-day trek is in my future, in which case, dynamic mode will be my preference. Actually, in that scenario, I'd probably opt for something more rugged, like the Garmin Instinct 3, to log my efforts instead.

But for everyday jogs, bike rides, dog walks, urban hikes, and other casual, quick workouts where I don't want the bulk of a smartphone weighing me down, you can bet I'll be sticking with the onboard GPS.

One of Roku's most popular screensavers is about to make its last splash. Here’s how to switch before Dec. 1.

A fan-favorite Roku screensaver is going away, and users aren’t happy.

Over the last several days, users with the Aquatic Life aquarium screensaver set as the default have noticed a message appearing when the screensaver opens. “Starting Dec. 1, 2026,” the message reads, “the Aquatic Life screensaver will no longer be available, and your screensaver will switch to Roku City.”

Also: The free Roku City screensaver game has me hooked

The screensaver, which displays a digital aquarium with tropical fish swimming back and forth, was available as a downloadable theme pack and was a popular pick for many years.

Users on Reddit quickly lamented the loss in many posts, with dozens noting that the aquarium was part of their daily routine. Roku responded to one post, saying, “That makes sense, and we hear you. Aquatic Life has a lot of loyal fans, and we’re passing your feedback along to the team.” The post noted that when “the fish swim off,” Roku devices with Aquatic Life will switch to Roku City.

You can browse to Settings > Theme > Screensaver to find another theme.

Several online reports indicate that the removal is a licensing issue and that the creator of the screensaver posted on Reddit that he removed the license after Roku’s sale to Fox. That thread has now been deleted, so the comment is unavailable. Roku hasn’t issued any statement of its own about why, but I have reached out to ask. If you’re looking for the exact screensaver, it’s still available as a 2-minute clip on Roku’s YouTube channel. Lastly, you can download the original app for your phone or computer from SereneScreen.

#3199. Scientists Build Biocomputer That Runs on Bacteria to Solve Hard Problems

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The study relied on the bacterium E. coli and V. natriegens to run the calculations.

Move over, microchips. The next generation of supercomputing might just run on living bacteria. For 20 years, an international team of scientists has been developing a biocomputer that uses bacteria to process information. Scientists from McGill University in Montreal announced their findings on Nov. 3 and published a paper detailing the results earlier this year in Nature.

Researchers from Canada, Europe, the United Kingdom and Australia contributed to this work, which combines biology with computer science and engineering. The researchers say the resulting biocomputer could be used to solve problems that give standard computers a hard time.

“Electronic (sequential) computers are not meant, or designed, to solve decision trees,” Dan Nicolau, a McGill bioengineering professor and senior author for the research paper, told CNET via email.

Nicolau noted that if electronic computers are to solve these types of problems, the computers will need a lot of RAM.

The study relied on the bacterium Escherichia coli and Vibrio natriegens to run the calculations. The researchers used E. coli because it moves through fluid in a predictable, measurable way and V. natriegens because it reproduces very quickly.

By using live bacteria rather than digital processing, the team says the biocomputer can solve big, complex problems at a small fraction of the memory and resources that regular computers require.

The researchers tested the biocomputer with a seemingly simple math problem called the Subset Sum Problem, which famously becomes exponentially harder as the number of inputs increases.

When the Subset Sum Problem inputs grow too large, the problem is known to give traditional computers issues, such as taking centuries, or even millions of years, to solve the problem.

The researchers translated the problem into a graph that branches off into each possible combination of inputs. Next, the team created a tiny physical structure that mirrored the Subset Sum Problem graph.

Inside the structure, they built a network of tunnels to mirror the graph branches. Each fork in the tunnels represents a decision point, and every possible route through the tunnels represents a different solution to the problem.

The researchers unleashed bacteria, which rapidly reproduce, inside the tunnels. The fast-growing bacteria moved through the tunnels, exploring many routes to the solution simultaneously.

Compared to digital processing, the bacteria are slow. But rather than tackling a problem sequentially, as traditional computers do, the bacteria can examine many solutions at once. And if you need more computing power, bacterial reproduction within the tunnels creates additional processing units to help solve the problem.

The team used automated image analysis to follow the bacteria through the correct tunnels. In this way, the researchers were able to tell which paths through the network satisfied the problem’s constraints.

The researchers were also able to adjust temperatures to prevent bacteria overcrowding while traveling through the network.

Enterprising fans have figured out how to run Doom, the groundbreaking 1993 first-person shooter video game, on everything from E. coli to a thermostat. Nicolau says Doom could probably run on the new system, with an important caveat concerning the biocomputer’s size.

“(The biocomputer) must be huge!” Nicolau said. Because bacteria make slow processors, you would need a massive biocomputer to host enough bacteria to run a video game.

But because no RAM is needed, Nicolau said biocomputing could help to solve the global RAM shortage, and even broaden our understanding of what a computer could be.

“A computer is a device which accepts (input) numbers and gets out (output) numbers. Full stop,” he said. “All other uses of the word computer (are) from our point of view, well, poetical.”

#3198. Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – most are free

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC (and the ones I keep)

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.

Revenue increased to $9.5 million from $6.6 million in first quarter, and the business is contributing margins that are accretive to the portfolio. A key focus has been sales excellence. The team is following a more rigorous process to help customers understand the technology, validate its application, and move towards an order. We are seeing the time from request for quotation to order shorten, alongside greater demand for larger machines and higher value purchase orders. The key message is the shift towards production. As customers move from evaluating the technology to using it in production, the scale and the opportunity expands.

That is why we remain particularly excited about the MEGA platform and the potential to introduce FlackTek's advanced materials processing technologies to the world. FlackTek is also a useful example of how we approach M&A. We look for differentiated, engineer-led businesses with proprietary technology that can expand our addressable markets and create opportunities for profitable growth. Alongside our investments in technologies such as Xdot, our focus is on turning technical differentiation into commercial results. Turning to operational excellence on slide five, our focus continues to move from not only building capabilities, but to getting more out of those capabilities as well.

The Navy and X-ray facilities in Batavia, automated welding, expanded assembly and testing in Colorado, and the cryogenic testing facility in Florida give us a stronger base from which to serve our customers. We are also continuing to modernize our systems through our ERP initiatives. The next step is to translate those capabilities into higher utilization, shortened cycle times, and improved throughput. The operational improvements contributing to this quarter's gross margin are encouraging, and we see further opportunity as we repeat that execution across more programs. During the quarter, we broke ground on our new 30,000 sq ft facility at our Arvada campus. This expansion is intended to support increasing demand and provide additional capacity for our turbomachinery applications.

It is an investment in our ability to execute the work ahead of us and support future growth. We continue to evaluate special capital projects against our 20% ROIC hurdle rate. Our focus is on investments that expand capacity, improve productivity, and strengthen differentiated capabilities. The change in our capital expenditure outlook reflects the timing of major projects, which Chris will discuss in more detail. These investments support the execution and visibility of our backlog, which increased 12% from a year ago and represents our seventh consecutive quarter of record backlog. Approximately 83% is in defense, with many programs extending over multiple years.

Our year-to-date book-to-bill is 1.2x, together with our active pipeline, supports our confidence in the fiscal 2027 outlook and our longer-term framework. As we move into the second half, we will build on these opportunities in space, defense, and expand aftermarket support, commercialize our proprietary technologies, and improve profitability through disciplined pricing. We also remain selective as we pursue acquisitions that complement our organic growth strategy and offer attractive returns. The foundation we have built is contributing more meaningfully to our results. We are pleased with our progress through the first half of the fiscal year and recognize there is more work ahead as we continue improving execution and creating value for our customers and shareholders.

I want to thank every one of our employees for their continued commitment to our customers and seeing our vision come to life. With that, I'll turn the call over to Chris for a detailed review of our financial results and outlook. Chris?

#3196. Open-Source Dependencies: 19 Trust Signals Worth Checking

Open-source libraries power much of today’s software, allowing developers to build on existing code rather than start from scratch. But every dependency a team adds also brings potential risks tied to its maintainers, the software it relies on, and how security issues are handled. Popularity and download counts can create a false sense of safety, and even a widely used package may be neglected or slow to receive security fixes.

Knowing what to look for before adding or retaining a dependency can mean the difference between a solid foundation and an inherited liability. Here, members of Forbes Technology Council share the trust signals teams should evaluate when choosing open-source dependencies or reviewing those already in use.

Check the transitive dependency footprint. A tiny package that pulls in dozens of libraries, install scripts or native binaries expands your attack surface far beyond the code you chose. Trust is not only about the package itself; it is about the chain of code and maintainers you inherit with it. Prefer the smallest dependency graph that solves the problem. - Alexandro Picolini, COMM

I’d evaluate how safely the project development is going. A reliable dependency should have planned releases, proper migration procedures and no surprises with breaking changes. While security is very important, stability is equally vital. When every update is an engineering challenge, the dependency will silently turn into tech debt despite its popularity. - Ajay Pandey

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

One critical trust signal is verifiable software provenance. Teams should know who maintains a dependency, how releases are built and signed, and whether artifacts can be traced to trusted source code. Popularity and download counts are not security guarantees. Provenance verification, combined with continuous vulnerability monitoring, strengthens software supply chain resilience. - Sai Krishna Manohar Cheemakurthi, U.S. Bank

First, run it through OpenSSF Scorecard. It’s a useful, free and automated check of practices that covers branch protection, code review, pinned dependencies and signed releases. A low score isn’t automatically disqualifying, but it can tell you what risk you’re inheriting and give every team the same repeatable bar instead of a gut feel based on GitHub stars. It’s one tool you can use to evaluate and get consistent results for open-source software. - Dan Sorensen, Nexus Security Advisors

Check when the maintainer last responded to a reported vulnerability, not when they last pushed code. Commit frequency tells you the project is alive. Response behavior tells you whether someone is actually watching the door. A repository with 10,000 stars and an 18-month-old unresolved security issue is not a dependency—it is a liability with good documentation. - Mukul Arora, Persistent Systems Limited

Examine who gets to become a maintainer. Attackers have learned it is easier to earn a tired maintainer’s trust over months than to find a flaw in the code. Check whether new maintainers are vetted by more than one person and whether handoffs happen in public. A project’s process for trusting people matters as much as its code. - Flavius Plesu, OutThink

One trust signal I’ve observed is how maintainers respond to reported security issues. It’s critical to look for clear updates and evidence that they fix problems rather than relying on download counts. A popular dependency can still leave your team waiting for a fix. - Mark Vena, SmartTech Research

The most useful trust signal is the patch track record. With AI now finding vulnerabilities in open source faster than ever, the question is no longer whether a flaw will be found but how quickly it can be fixed once it is found. Teams should look at the dependency’s current vulnerability history and update cadence and determine whether maintainers respond rapidly to security issues. A modern software project that is popular but patches slowly should be avoided in the AI era. - Anuj Goel, Cyware

Check who is actually maintaining it. A popular library with millions of downloads can still rest on one unpaid volunteer who hasn’t merged a fix in a year. Look at recent commit activity, how quickly security issues get patched, and how many active maintainers there are. Download counts measure popularity, not durability, and you’re inheriting the support risk. - Steven Singer, Arbill

Open source runs on shared ingenuity. Give that ingenuity a security check: look for a current assessment of the exact package version you’ll deploy, inspecting its contents for malware, tampering and suspicious behavior alongside known vulnerabilities. Check each update and reassess existing dependencies as threats emerge. Trust the community, and give it the backup it deserves. - Mario Vuksan, ReversingLabs

Look at support and usage. Open source is great in terms of lesser cost and general support, but with general support, there is more risk. An open-source project can have security flaws or problematic issues that are not easily spotted by even the most advanced professionals. Look for something that serves one purpose and has been proven before by use in other high-profile projects or companies. Then go for it—with contingencies in place. - WaiJe Coler, InfoTracer

A useful signal is whether another party can rebuild the published release from the tagged source and get the same artifact. Signed provenance says who claims to have built it; reproducibility lets an independent team check that claim without trusting the maintainer’s pipeline. Before adoption, try this on one release and see whether the project documents the toolchain, inputs and steps needed to repeat the build. This makes artifact integrity independently testable. - Jagadish Gokavarapu, Wissen Infotech

A trustworthy project actively updates its own upstream dependencies, maintains clear semantic versioning, and demonstrates steady commit velocity. If a library has millions of downloads but hasn’t shipped a patch or addressed security pull requests in six months, its technical debt becomes yours the moment you import it. - Japjeev Kohli, Transurban

Look for active community adoption and scrutiny. Widely used, actively maintained packages benefit from more people reviewing, testing and finding problems. I would also avoid automatically adopting a new release on day one. Give the community time to validate it before bringing it into a critical environment. - Alex Spokoiny, Check Point Software

Ask who chose it. More dependencies now arrive because a model suggested them, not because an engineer compared options. At Google, adding a dependency meant someone had to argue for it and own it afterward. That argument is the trust signal. If nobody on the team can say why this package is better than the alternatives, you have not evaluated a dependency. You have accepted a recommendation. - Prashant Jalan, Guickly

I’d look at whether the project has an active, healthy maintainer community. Not all open-source projects are resilient. A dependency can be technically excellent yet still introduce risk if it’s maintained by only one or two individuals, receives infrequent updates, or lacks clear governance. Healthy open-source projects tend to show consistent releases, responsive issue management, transparent security practices and a diverse contributor base. - Ciaran Cosgrave, Nearform

Read the license on the model weights, not only on the code. Teams now pull open-weight AI models into products the way they pull in libraries, and some of those licenses ban commercial use, cap the number of users, or restrict whole categories of use. The code around a model can carry an MIT license, while the weights you ship come with different terms. - Jerry Tang, Atlas Cloud

One key trust signal is whether an open-source dependency creates accurate and consistent results. Libraries used in calculations, data conversion or scientific computing can cause errors that affect major decisions. Test key functions against trusted reference results and check for rounding errors or erratic outputs. A package may meet security standards but still produce wrong results. Trust must include functional accuracy, not just security and maintenance. - Salice Thomas, Wipro Limited

Essentially, I look for good governance signals. How large and spread out is the group of top maintainers—the more coherent, the better—and what’s their relationship with the project? How fast do they fix issues, especially security issues? Are security tests embedded in the build and release pipelines? Are there external security validations like OpenSSF? #3195. Data Center Backers Suffer Near-Total Midterm Defeats Across the Country

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

More than 40 voting initiatives yielded almost nothing but resistance to data-center projects.

The 2026 midterm election blue wave, which shifted the balance of power in Congress and across state races toward Democrats, can be seen as a repudiation of AI and the controversial data centers that provide its computing power. Data center proponents have heavily backed President Donald Trump and Republican candidates, underscored by xAI CEO Elon Musk investing hundreds of millions of dollars into Texas midterm campaigns to support the industry.

But in many parts of the country, voters didn’t need to make their voices on data centers heard through candidates. They had direct initiatives on the ballot this week that would decide whether data center projects would move ahead in their districts.

In line with a growing backlash against data centers and AI, voters supported about 40 election-day measures that would restrict the construction of new data centers, with only one result — in Harwood, North Dakota — favoring data center expansion.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

As broken down by the website Data Centers on the Ballot, Ohio had the most number of voting measures: 21, all of which were in favor of restrictions.

Maine, Illinois, Kansas, New Jersey, California, Florida, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin were the other states with data center voting.

Six elections were held earlier in 2026 in California, Michigan, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, with all of them finding voters opposed to allowing data center builds to continue without new restrictions.

Not all the proposed restrictions were the same. In some elections, voters decided whether to impose a megawatt cap on data center energy use, while other measures addressed specific zoning issues or whether data center projects should require voter approval. Some proposed an outright ban on new data centers, and six of those were successful.

Polls by groups including Pew Research have found Americans have soured on data centers due to high electricity bills, water use and environmental concerns, among other reasons. It’s also hard to separate concerns about data centers from concerns about AI affecting jobs. AI has also become a divisive enough issue to affect midterm voting.

The election results were so bad for the industry that Politico declared data centers to be “the midterms’ other big loser” next to Republicans. Not only did voters enact additional restrictions on builds across the country, but data centers were mentioned in Democratic victory speeches.

“I do not work for data centers. I do not work for Wall Street. I work for you, I work for Ohio,” Senator-elect Sherrod Brown said in his victory speech Tuesday night.

USA Today reported that two mayors, one in Oklahoma and one in Ohio, were recalled after public backlash over proposed data centers.

The midterms might have longer-term effects for tech companies and data center firms. It’s likely that with Democratic control of Congress, there’ll be more scrutiny.

“Public policy is going to reflect public opinion, and there’s been a very substantial change in public opinion just over the last year,” Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Politico.

Political headwinds from the midterms could lead local officials across the country to gain public favor by delaying or canceling data center projects or putting pressure on the companies behind them to offer more attractive deals to communities. The days of huge tax breaks and incentives for data centers could be coming to a close.

“Now, (communities) are pushing data centers to pay taxes, create their own power plants, pay for their use of electricity and water and contribute to local community resources like education funds,” The New York Times reported.

#3194. I tried Sonos’ latest app features – these 2 small upgrades fix big annoyances

Also: Sonos Ace Ultra vs. Sonos Ace: Who should upgrade

This time, Sonos added System Health, a new in-app page to access a more comprehensive view of your system(s), though it’s only available on iOS for now. However, a new blog post states that iOS and Android users can expect volume presets, more interaction with the app miniplayer, and spoken voice prompts for the Ace Ultra headphones.

I poked around in the app and tried some of the latest features. Here’s what to expect.

If your system consists of multiple speakers, a mix of modern and legacy speakers, or multiple systems, you’re bound to experience a hiccup and be unsure which speaker is causing the issue.

It usually takes me some time to Google my issue and scroll through the Sonos Community forum, Reddit, or the official Sonos help documents to find suggestions and troubleshoot it. Sonos’ new System Health feature provides an overview of your systems, showing your network status and name, as well as the number of speakers and rooms in each system.

Also: I used Sonos’s new home theater feature – it’s a competition killer

According to Sonos’ blog post, System Health can detect a Double Network Address issue, which usually occurs when you introduce a new router to your home or plug a mesh system into your ISP-provided router. The result is two home networks, and your Sonos speakers will split their connection between them, flagging “System not found” errors, missing speakers, or connection dropouts.

System Health is in the Settings tab, under the Help Center menu.

Once you tap into your system, you can see all of its speakers, with unconnected speakers bearing a red “Not connected” badge, and wireless speakers showing a black “Powered off” badge when they’re off.

Then, you can see a speaker’s connection information, including status, Wi-Fi signal strength, signal/noise ratio, frequency, IP address, and more. You can also find its volume output, Trueplay setup status, line-in connection, voice control status, serial number, hardware model and version, and which Sonos platform it operates on.

System Health can also show you your account details, Sonos ID, Controller ID, and your current app build version. System Health comes after Sonos updated the System Updates tab, which now displays an overview of your app, system, and headphone update status. This page also links to the Sonos release notes.

Sonos’ blog post states that this feature is new and still open to change, especially if the Sonos community has a particularly overwhelming response to it. The blog post also disclaims that this feature is a first look, not a deep dive.

However, after a brief first use, I see it as a great way to quickly access all the details you need about your systems and speakers, especially if you’re doing some rewiring, moving a speaker to a new room, or general troubleshooting.

System Health is rolling out to iOS users first. I updated my Sonos app in the App Store and was able to access it, but Sonos’ blog post states that this update is a phased rollout.

Updates to the Sonos app and its player are a long time coming. After receiving several new ways to control your speakers’ volume (I think we’re up to three), Sonos is realizing that granular volume control is a high priority for many Sonos users, including me.

The in-app volume dial is cool, and the interactive volume scrubber is a nice touch, but there’s nothing more jarring than wanting to play some tunes on my kitchen counter speaker, only for it to blast at 80% from when my husband was watching football the night before.

Sonos’ latest big update to volume this time around is Presets, a way to start playback in a specific room at a set volume. I haven’t found this feature in my app’s update yet, but I think it’s because my hardware needs an update. Presets will be available on iOS and Android.

Fortunately, I did use another update to the Sonos miniplayer: swipe to skip. What a teeny, tiny but useful feature. It works just like the miniplayer in Apple Music and Spotify; when the app is open, you can swipe left to skip to the next song.

One major caveat: swiping right to replay a track doesn’t work — at least not yet. Swiping both ways seems like a given to me, so it feels odd that you can’t. Still, being able to swipe the miniplayer to the next track is better than always having the main player open to toggle tracks. This feature is also coming to iOS and Android.

Sonos’ miniplayer is getting so much better; you can swipe to the next track and easily control volume from it, even when you have the Ace or Ace Ultra connected (I tried). The in-app volume dial also works with Sonos headphones.

Also: Sonos Play vs. Sonos Move 2: Why I’d go with the $200 cheaper Bluetooth speaker

Speaking of the Ace Ultra, a firmware update is available. A new Vocal Guidance feature can announce the battery percentage when you power on the headphones, when the audio mode changes from ANC to Transparency, and which device your headphones are connected to via Bluetooth.

It feels like this update is the final stretch before Sonos 27voice arrives, as the release notes suggest. It appears Sonos is laying the groundwork for speakers to support the AI-powered voice assistant in Early Access. Once it’s here, I’ll test it as soon as I can.

#3192. Tokens Built The Digital AI Business. Physical AI Needs A Different Unit

Brandon Barbello is co-founder and COO of Archetype AI, with over 10 years of product leadership across Fortune 500 and startups.

​Almost every industrial AI deployment I’ve seen lately eventually reaches the same meeting. The pilot worked, the operations team wants to expand to more machines and finance asks what the numbers look like at 300 assets instead of three.

Increasingly, that question comes with another: Will you charge us by the token?​

Enterprises have spent the past few years learning a new vocabulary around AI economics: tokens, inference, context windows, consumption-based pricing and discovering how hard those costs are to predict. Accenture recently reported that one in three organizations exhausts its AI token budget before year’s end.​

For digital AI, token economics are justifiable. Jensen Huang has said he’d be “deeply alarmed” if a $500,000 engineer didn’t consume at least $250,000 of tokens a year, because the spend buys output. For knowledge work, he’s right.​

But a compressor is not a $500,000 engineer. It produces signal every second it runs, regardless of whether anyone asks it a question. It makes more sense to analyze that signal locally, on hardware the customer already owns, than to ship every second of it to the cloud.​

We have an opportunity to build business models that reflect those differences instead of importing LLM economics into the physical world.​

Most LLM interactions are episodic: A person asks a question or gives an agent a task, and the model produces an output.

In the physical world, cameras, vibration monitors, pressure gauges and other sensors generate data continuously, and applications are inherently always-on. Meter by the token, and the bill grows with every hour the equipment runs.

The underlying data is different, too. Language models are trained on text and images. They don’t understand what a bearing sounds like at 4,000 RPM. That takes a model built to interpret physical signals directly.​

Industrial data is also often too proprietary to leave the facility. Streaming that data to the cloud puts the company’s core IP at risk. This affects how physical AI gets deployed, scaled and priced.​

The practical answer is to run intelligence where the data originates. Smaller, general-purpose models can increasingly run on customers’ own hardware, keeping sensitive information on-site and letting decisions happen where the data is produced.

One municipal customer of Archetype AI, for example, uses cameras across hundreds of intersections to improve pedestrian safety. Based on internal analysis, each intersection produces roughly 43 gigabytes of camera data daily. Moving that data to the cloud would cost an estimated $850,000 to $1 million annually before any AI processing. Distilling a larger model into a smaller one let physical AI run on hardware the customer already owns, using its existing cameras.​​

Running at the edge, the system can determine if a pedestrian is still in the crosswalk without sending data to a remote data center and waiting for a response. That round trip could take longer than the window to act.

Training, fine-tuning and fleet-level analysis can continue to happen in the cloud, while time-sensitive decisions happen closer to the edge. Use the cloud where scale is valuable and the edge where speed, cost and responsiveness matter most.​

When AI runs primarily as a metered cloud service, consumption-based pricing makes sense: Someone has to pay for the compute.

But once physical AI runs on the customer’s infrastructure, compute is already paid for, so pricing doesn’t have to correspond to every unit of inference. It can follow from the unit where the customer actually receives value.​ Industrial businesses already think this way, and it’s how they buy software.

This points to a different model: licensing per asset, machine, facility or application, rather than charging when the system processes data. That brings predictability. Finance teams can count machines more easily than forecast tokens; a company expanding from 10 machines to 1,000 knows the cost before deployment.​​

The operational value becomes clearer at scale. In one Archetype AI customer deployment, analysis of data from more than 40 sensors across 63 wind turbines identified nine previously unknown failure modes, revealing critical problems before they cause downtime.​

The trade-off is that per-asset licensing can be less economical for equipment that needs only occasional analysis. Companies should consider how often the system will be used and the operational value it delivers.​

Inference is getting cheaper. Gartner predicts inference on a one-trillion-parameter model will cost providers over 90% less by 2030 than in 2025. Elsewhere, however, Gartner expects inference spend per agentic workflow to climb more than fivefold through 2028, since agentic systems use five to 30 times more tokens per task than chatbots.

In other words, falling unit costs don’t guarantee savings. Every new sensor adds volume, regardless of operational value.

NVIDIA researchers argue that smaller LLMs are already powerful and economical enough for many agentic tasks. Physical AI takes that further, with models built from the start to understand physical signals and run where signals originate.​

Physical AI is still in early days. We shouldn’t assume what worked for digital AI is right for physical. Pricing per asset means vendors grow as customers expand, and customers expand as the system proves its value.

Before expanding a pilot, businesses can bring operations, IT and finance together to compare the total cost at three assets, 30 and 300, including licensing, hardware, integration and ongoing support. Weigh those costs against measurable outcomes such as reduced downtime or maintenance hours, and agree on what would justify expansion.

When finance understands what 300 assets will cost and operations can demonstrate the value, the conversation can move from how usage will be billed to whether—and how quickly—to scale.​​​

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

#3186. Himax Blames 'Abrupt and Significant Correction' in Auto Chip Demand as Stock Crashes Nearly 30%. Is Now the Time to Buy?

Himax sees fourth-quarter revenue falling 22% to 26% after a sudden pullback in auto chips. Is the slump temporary?

Himax (HIMX -26.44%), the fabless chip designer behind display driver chips for TVs, phones and car screens, expects a steep revenue drop in the final quarter of the year, and investors are punishing the stock amid an already bruising day for the market.

On the company's earnings call Thursday, President and CEO Jordan Wu blamed "an abrupt and significant correction" in automotive display driver chip orders for the new guidance. Shares had plunged nearly 28% to $7.55 by about 2:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, a steep decline exacerbated by a broader market sell-off targeting AI-linked names.

Wu told the call that the year began soft in the first quarter. Panel makers then bought heavily in the second and third quarters to keep up with surging orders from Chinese automakers expanding overseas. "Right after China's National Day holidays in early October," he said, the company saw a "sudden and sizable decline in demand among the customers that had purchased aggressively in prior quarters."Wu also said the forecast cut partly reflects Chinese automakers' "earlier, overly aggressive export expectations, along with their growing concerns over inventory levels across distribution channels." He added that panel makers mostly serving customers outside China have held their forecasts steady, and some have nudged fourth-quarter orders higher.The damage is concentrated in automotive display drivers. Wu said automotive timing-controller sales should keep growing from quarter to quarter.That earlier buying spree already showed up in the third quarter. Automotive driver sales rose in solid double digits from the prior quarter, marking the second straight quarter of strong growth, as some panel makers accelerated purchases.

Third-quarter revenue rose 8.5% to $246.8 million from the prior quarter, and gross margin improved to 34.2% from 33.1%. Profit came to $18.6 million, or 10.7 cents per diluted ADS (American depositary share), topping the company's 8 to 10-cent guidance, which Himax attributed to lower-than-expected operating expenses.For the fourth quarter, management expects gross margin flat to slightly up and profit of 4.5 to 6.5 cents per diluted ADS. That range leaves out an expected after-tax gain of about $19 to $20 million from selling its stake in an equity-method investment, a sale Himax expects to close this quarter.

Wu said on the call that automotive chip sales rose a "decent" 16% year over year in the first nine months of 2026, and he still expects about 10% growth for the full year, even with worldwide vehicle production expected to decline. The company also expects automotive timing-controller sales to grow more than 40% this year. Non-driver sales, which include timing controllers, reached $51.0 million in the third quarter, up 11.2% from the prior quarter.The chief executive framed the slump as "abrupt, short-term order adjustments by certain customers, while our market leader position remains firmly intact."Supply is the other theme. Wu said foundries and packaging and testing providers have announced significant price increases for 2027 and that capacity is the company's top priority because automotive customers demand stricter supply assurance. He added that Himax has secured capacity commitments from key suppliers and is working with customers to share rising costs. However, higher foundry prices will remain a cost to watch, with Himax and across tech stocks that rely on outside chipmakers.

It depends on how you read October. If customers simply over-ordered and are now working through inventory, the full-year automotive growth target suggests the business is intact, and that's how management describes it. If end demand for Chinese car exports is weaker than implied by those orders, the correction could run longer than a quarter.With the stock down so steeply in Thursday trading, a lot of bad news may already be priced in, particularly since it appears investors are fearing the worst when it comes to how a newly elected government could interfere with the AI build-out. Even so, a sudden guidance cut does warrant caution. Many long-term investors would likely wait for evidence that the fourth-quarter outlook holds, and anyone interested in these semiconductor stocks might keep a position small.The next checkpoints are whether fourth-quarter profit lands in the guided 4.5 to 6.5 cent range and whether the stake sale closes as expected.

None of these are exactly an all-purpose cleaner (as may be obvious with staples such as tomato paste, below), but for specific jobs, in the absence of the perfect product, or to spite the industrial cleaning complex that would have you believe there is a perfect product, the solution or anecdote may already be lurking in your cupboards.

Using that which you already have on hand is a win-win-win. You’ll feel like a mastermind, save money and avoid the tyranny of more and more plastic. “The most sustainable cleaner is usually the one already in your kitchen, says Julian Silva, founder of Plastno nontoxic cleaners, “because you skip buying another single-purpose bottle.”

To use pantry products for cleaning and polishing, “It’s helpful to figure out why a certain product or method works in order to better determine other applications,” says Sofia Martinez, cleaning expert and owner of Sparkly Maid Austin. She also cautions, however, “Disinfecting is not the same as cleaning. Just because a product or method removes soil, provides shine or covers up odor doesn’t mean that the surface has been properly disinfected.”

Silva, Martinez and other cleaning experts below explain why and share seven kitchen staples you probably already have on hand that can clean or polish.

Polishing and disinfecting are far from the same thing, but the kitchen staple you might have sitting right next to your stove can also add shine.

“Olive oil can make fingerprints on stainless-steel appliances much less noticeable, because it creates an ultra-thin coating that changes how light reflects off the surface and disguises smudges,” says Raquel Perez, owner of Karen’s Green Maids in Chicago.

You’re not going to want to use large quantities of oil to clean up the oil and other foodstuffs that spatter during cooking, obviously. “Only use a tiny drop,” Perez advises. “Rub it onto a microfiber cloth, and always test on a small, hidden area first. Too much will make it feel greasy.”

Tomato paste isn’t exactly something like baking soda, where you might confidently apply it to whatever and see if it works. “I would describe tomato paste as a very limited tarnish removal option, not an all-purpose cleaner,” says Martinez. In other words, don’t rub deeply colored, concentrated tomatoes on your cutting boards and countertops.

However, it might do the trick for polishing stainless steel, copper pots and pans, or brass fixtures. “Its acidity can help loosen some oxidation,” she says, “while its thick consistency helps the paste stay in contact with the surface.” As with just about everything here, try a small amount on an out-of-the-way spot first.

Soaking up excess oil with bread is the kind of hack that deserves its own headline. (See here.) You can also use it in place of a broom when something shatters.

“Soft bread is great for broken glass because the crumb grabs the tiny shards a broom misses,” says Silva. “Carefully pick up the big pieces first, then press a slice over the area and toss it right after.” Make sure to press, not rub, as rubbing can cause bigger problems and small scratches. Disposing of it right away, and deep in the trash, is also crucial so nobody (including pets) mistakes it for something they could eat as a snack or croutons.

Your sink may be the basin you use for rinsing and cleaning, but grime and soap residue can build up in certain places and require cleaning. For a quick fix that requires less elbow grease and leaves your stainless steel sink shiny, turn to your baking supplies.

“Sprinkle a little flour over a clean, dry sink and rub it around with a soft, dry cloth or paper towel to remove residual grime and give it a polished look,” says Sham Zemichael, owner and operations manager of Costina Cleaning Services. Conditions must be right in order to begin here, though. “Note that this can backfire if you do it over a damp sink,” he says. “You’ll be left with a flour slurry and more grime than there was before. I use it as a finishing touch on washed and completely dried sinks, and I also recommend keeping the flour away from the drain to avoid it clumping in there.”

Cream of tartar might be one of those baking supplies that sits in the back of your cabinet for years (decades?) because it’s used only for highly specific baking projects. If you’re not regularly stabilizing egg whites in your kitchen or using it as a baking soda sidekick, try using it up before the best-by date by giving it another purpose.

“Most of those gray ‘scratches’ on ceramic plates and sinks are actually metal left behind by forks and knives, since the glaze is harder than the cutlery,” says Silva. “Cream of tartar mixed into a paste with a little water is a gentle, mildly acidic abrasive, so it rubs that metal off without hurting the glaze.” It won’t fix a true scratch, but it will give old ceramics a smart look when they just need a little glow-up.

Seasoning cast iron is a process unto itself, giving its heavyweight, heat-retaining base what is essentially a nonstick surface. Even if you consistently give your cast iron the white-glove treatment in care and cleaning, little rust spots can still appear here and there. You don’t always have to start over with the full seasoning process when this happens, however.

“My favorite way of cleaning light surface rust on cast iron is dipping a half-cut potato in baking soda and rubbing it over the rusty patches,” Zemichael says. “The small amounts of oxalic acid inside potatoes help loosen rust buildup, and the baking soda acts as a mild abrasive for a cleaner finish,” he says. “It doesn’t work for stubborn rust, though. I simply use it for new spots when they appear.”

For kitchen tables or coffee tables that have been begging you to use coasters, you may be able to minimize water rings with what you have on hand for sandwiches. “Mayonnaise can help with water ring stains in some types of wood,” says Perez. “Before trying this solution, find out what type of wood finish your table has and how deep the water-ring stain goes,” she says, whether it’s just in the finish or goes deeper. “That will affect how you should try to remove it and avoid making the situation worse.”

The vegetable oil in full-fat mayonnaise can help displace the moisture that’s locked inside the finish. Apply a thin coating to the ring and let it sit for at least 15 minutes or overnight, covered with plastic wrap. Wipe with a clean, dry cloth after the mayo has absorbed the moisture.

White or hazy rings are worth trying this on, but darker rings might be beyond help. “The mayo can affect the appearance of the stain, as opposed to removing it,” says Perez, and you could be left with a greasy area around the stain if it’s not completely removed.

#3184. SUSE lays off 1 in 10 workers – citing AI and automation

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Squarespace also announced layoffs this week, but explicit ties to AI remain inconsistent.

According to exclusive reporting by The Register, enterprise Linux provider SUSE will lay off one in 10 of its nearly 2,000-person workforce due to “automation and AI,” CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen told staff via email.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI?

Van Leeuwen noted that AI is rapidly changing how software companies function.

“AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work,” he said, adding that “the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully.”

He did not specify which roles would be terminated, but The Register reports that staff will be notified by Nov. 4.

AI is impacting many parts of the tech industry, including open source. Just last month, Linus Torvalds announced he had used Claude Code to write a Linux patch, which Linux enthusiasts read as an evolution of his stance on AI.

By some reports, businesses are finally seeing some ROI from AI after a few years of uncertainty. But that remains localized, ironically, to tech itself. As one economist recently noted, AI has primarily increased revenue per employee at major tech companies, while leaving most other companies unchanged.

The trade-off for that growth is, at least in some cases, layoffs. But layoffs credited to AI in some way don’t mean that human roles are always being replaced. Last month, Microsoft announced it would buy out 60,000 of its workers — some of which are in its Copilot division — to prioritize AI efforts, though it’s also likely the company is reacting to spending a significant amount of money on AI infrastructure.

Jobloss.ai’s layoff tracker shows primarily tech companies — including Uber, Salesforce, and GitLab — in its recent entries, but job loss attribution to AI is still mixed, and the number of roles cut isn’t always jarringly huge.

It’s also hard to tell whether a layoff strategically frames pre-AI plans as being due to AI capabilities or is actually a result of them. That question circulated around Block’s major layoffs earlier this year. Squarespace also announced layoffs of 19% of its staff yesterday, though company communications don’t explicitly name AI. Still, vibecoding has impacted website builders overall, though Squarespace itself has invested in AI offerings.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires

Van Leeuwen’s email to staff acknowledged where SUSE has already begun to change, though it’s unclear whether he meant by adopting AI tools internally.

“Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years,” he said.

While several tech companies have announced highly visible layoffs this year that they’ve also framed as related to AI, economists agree that the massive cross-industry layoff wave many fear has yet to arrive. Gartner even predicts that companies will actually rehire 30% of the employees they tried to replace with AI — and at a higher cost — by 2029 if they don’t “overhaul workforce planning.”

Still, AI investments, vibecoding, and shifting priorities are changing the software scene overall.

#3182. A New Water Heater Technology Kills Bacteria Right in the Tank

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I asked the inventor about his design and when consumers might see the tech in their homes.

One challenge of current water heater designs is staying hot enough to kill harmful bacteria like Legionella pneumophila, which can cause Legionnaires’ disease. A new water heater design, developed and patented by researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, aims to raise tank temperatures to 160 degrees Fahrenheit, which spells instant doom for Legionella bacteria.

Legionella bacteria love warm water, so while they struggle to survive in a water heater tank set to 120 F, they’re more than comfortable elsewhere in a home’s hot water pipes. It’s technically possible to achieve sufficient temperatures with existing water heaters, but those temperatures are also likely to scald human skin whenever you turn on the faucet.

The biggest innovation of this new design is how it finds a new use for heat exchangers, the same technology behind air conditioners, heat pumps, furnaces and refrigerators. I wanted to know more, so I reached out to David Yashar, a NIST mechanical engineer behind the new design.

As Yashar and his team researched ways to kill Legionella bacteria, they needed to figure out how to make tank temperatures around 160 F safe and practical for humans. They ultimately landed on the concept of using cold water entering the water heater to cool the hot water leaving the tank with an unmixed heat exchanger that contains the water inlet and outlet.

The principle behind unmixed heat exchangers—where the fluids don’t mix—is that incoming cold water gets a heating boost from the hot-water outlet while cooling the water to safe levels for people. As a result, the tank can maintain the high temperatures required to prevent pathogen growth behind illnesses like Legionnaires’ disease, which has a fatality rate of around 10%, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Beyond the safety benefits, the process recaptures some waste heat and can improve heating efficiency for the cold water, since it enters the tank warmer.

I’ve covered various heating, ventilation and air conditioning tech over the years, so I immediately recognized similarities between the new design’s unmixed heat exchanger and those used in HVAC and refrigerators. For example, air conditioners use a heat exchanger for the refrigeration cycle (also called the Carnot cycle) to pull heat from air inside your home (evaporator coil) and push it outside (condenser coil) without pulling in outside air. Additionally, heat pumps may use a heat exchanger for defrosting ice buildup when in heating mode.

When I asked about the similarities, Yashar noted that it wasn’t a coincidence that his patent took inspiration from HVAC and refrigeration tech. Yashar said, “My background is in HVAC&R, and it is very common to use unmixed heat exchangers like this to manipulate the bounds of the Carnot cycle to achieve some specific condition. I came up with the idea when I first learned about Legionella and the existing mitigation strategies.” He goes on to explain that using an unmixed heat exchanger “across the inlet and outlet was a very simple, effective, and inexpensive way to push the water temperature up to that condition and back down.”

It’s fitting that Yashar discovered better ways for heat exchangers not only to kill pathogens, but also to improve energy efficiency. Finding new applications for existing technology is certainly an underrated aspect of invention.

As exciting as this tech is, a patent doesn’t necessarily mean it will hit the market immediately. Yashar notes that while his research “proved the concept using a 60-gallon tank,” it depends on when manufacturers license the technology and get their engineers working on designing consumer products suitable for homes. This process could happen quickly or take several years.

It may be years before we see consumer heaters that use the promising new technology.

Because Yashar’s concept essentially modified an existing water heater, I asked if it would be possible to retrofit products in people’s homes. He notes that NIST’s project started with the intention of modifying the tank’s hardware and controls. “The steps we took might not be simple tasks for an existing application,” said Yashar. “It really depends on a lot of things, so it is best if people learn how this works and understand how to achieve it within their existing application.”

He brings up one important consideration: Retrofit tanks will need extra insulation to be worth it. It’s “absolutely necessary for a retrofit because the tank temperature will be about 40 degrees hotter than what the existing system was designed for. If this isn’t done, the standby losses would be very large.” Without appropriate insulation, any efficiency gained by the heat exchanger would be lost to heat loss in standby mode.

So, while a retrofit might be possible, it seems more likely to engineer a product from the ground up based on this design, especially if consumers want to keep utility costs manageable.

For more tips, see the best temperature to set your thermostat this winter and learn how to find air leaks in your home for more efficient heating.

Mortgage rates are continuing to cool off as we head into November.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 6.93% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

A significant drop is eye-catching, but bear in mind that you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. Since September, mortgage rates have been hovering around 7%. That’s a full percentage point higher than they were at the beginning of 2026.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

#3179. Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are finally here, two months after Apple unveiled the always-listening Apple Watch features. Here's how they work.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind, Apple’s two controversial, always-listening Audio Intelligence features, are now available on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 with the iOS 27.3 developer beta. Both features are opt-in.

Apple unveiled Siri Recap and Live Rewind in September alongside its Series 12 and Ultra 4 smartwatches, but it waited to release the features until after the smartwatches launched. Siri Recap provides a high-level summary of meetings, while Live Rewind continuously buffers audio so the watch wearer can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds.

Also: Apple’s Audio Intelligence is priming us for its real AI wearable future

To try both features today, update your iPhone to the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and then update your Apple Watch.

Within the Siri app, users will find a new section called “Recaps,” where both the Siri Recaps and Live Rewinds live.

Siri Recap isn’t listening for nitty-gritty details within a meeting or recording a transcript’s worth of text. It’s more geared toward a conversation’s key takeaways, like important dates, times, prices, and action items. A demo of the feature showed an off-the-cuff conversation between a parent and a child discussing college application strategies. Siri Recap took notes on the high school activities the student could pursue to include in their application, the topics they could write about in their essay, and the colleges they could consider applying to.

After a conversation, a user can save the meeting notes in the Siri app or export them to Notes or Journal. If they don’t save the conversation, it’s automatically deleted after seven days.

Apple designed the feature to exclude certain information from the Siri Recap. It includes a person’s name only if they introduce themselves or if their name is regularly brought up in conversation. Otherwise, it avoids identifying speakers. It also scrubs the audio of language that promotes self-harm, financial and authentication data, and personal identifiers.

You can enable or disable Recaps at any time through Control Center. You can create something akin to a Focus mode to automatically enable the feature once your Apple Watch detects you’ve reached your office or college lecture. Each morning, Siri Recap sends a notification to alert you that the feature is on. At the end of each day, you get a reminder to check your daily recaps in the Siri app.

The feature constantly assesses whether a conversation is relevant, optimizing its detection based on the conversation’s context, proximity, and length. It pauses summarization when a user is on a phone or FaceTime call, plays music, or uses earbuds. It won’t work when Bluetooth devices like AirPods are in use.

Double-press the Digital Crown to see a transcript of the past 15 seconds of conversation. The Apple Watch chimes and displays an animation to indicate it’s in use, then shows the transcript for 30 seconds.

Also: Is cellular on Apple Watch worth it? 4 ways people use it – and why I opt out

Live Rewind is built for those head-in-the-clouds moments when you miss a tidbit of information and can’t go back and ask what a speaker said. I think about how useful this could be in a college lecture or boardroom setting, where dozens of people’s conversations and questions prevent someone from asking a clarifying question about what was discussed.

The user can send the snippet to the Siri app to save it or ask about it (if they want to look up the definition of a mentioned term or get more information on the history of a mentioned topic, for example). If the user doesn’t act on it, the snippet is deleted. Any snippet you save is encrypted through iCloud. The audio buffer updates continuously, and unused audio is automatically deleted. It’s processed on the device and not sent to Apple.

Think of the Secure Exclave as a private island on the S11 chip where the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 process audio. A secure audio buffer processes the raw audio, and a secure pairing mechanism privately enables the connection between a paired Apple Watch and iPhone.

Also: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 just hit its lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday

For Siri Recap, the S11 chip listens to detect whether the watch wearer is part of a current conversation. Once detected, audio enters the Secure Exclave, where it’s encrypted and sent to the Secure Exclave on the iPhone. The iPhone turns that audio into condensed text, essentially editing the conversation to remove filler words or irrelevant information, and then it’s sent to private cloud compute. Private cloud compute creates a recap, delivered to your iPhone’s Siri app.

This process ensures that no one, including Apple, can access the audio data.

Don’t want your Apple Watch to listen to you? Siri Recap and Live Rewind are off by default, according to Apple.

If your Apple Watch prompts you to enable Audio Intelligence during setup, you can choose which features to turn on.

On its support page, Apple said you can “turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone.” Once it’s enabled, you can “turn it on or off at any time from Control Center.” To enable Live Rewind, Apple said to “open the Watch app, tap Siri, then tap Live Rewind and turn on ‘Double Click Digital Crown.’”

I haven’t tested these controls myself. I’d expect you can follow the same steps to switch Live Rewind off, but I haven’t confirmed that yet.
