#3130. Prediction: This Will Be SpaceX's Stock Price by the End of 2029

SpaceX stock has the potential to quadruple in the next three years.

SpaceX (SPCX -9.05%) has quickly established itself as one of the most exciting stocks in the market. Given the company's growth, I think the stock could generate around $2 trillion in revenue by 2030 and end 2029 with a stock price of $570.

SpaceX is focused on the future, and it is pursuing some promising new markets, including orbital data centers, asteroid mining, and Earth-to-Earth cargo transport using suborbital rockets. The road to success in these areas will come down to the company being able to reliably recapture and reuse both stages of its Starship rockets after each launch. If it can pull off this feat, that will set the stage for it to pursue these loftier goals and accelerate its launch cadence.

The company's goal is for the Starship rocket -- a much larger platform than its current Falcon rockets -- to begin flying weekly in the first half of next year, and potentially twice a week starting in the second half of the year. If SpaceX can quickly recover, refurbish, and fully reuse its Starship rockets, it will be able to greatly increase the mass of the payloads it can carry and its number of revenue-generating launches, drastically altering space economics and leading to strong revenue growth in the coming years.

SpaceX is also eyeing disruption of some current industries, like the U.S. mobile phone market. The Starlink satellite broadband business will continue to be a nice revenue driver in the coming years as SpaceX continues to add new commercial, enterprise, and government customers. However, building out a full terrestrial cellphone network would likely take four to six years, so this is more of a medium-term opportunity.

Another growth driver will be AI coding, thanks to SpaceX's recent acquisition of Cursor. Cursor is essentially a workflow interface that can use both its own and third-party AI models to help users write, edit, debug, and review code. Morgan Stanley projects that as a part of SpaceX, Cursor's annual recurring revenue (ARR) will climb from $8 billion at the end of 2026 to roughly $33 billion by the end of 2030.

SpaceX's biggest growth opportunity, however, is likely to come from artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. The company is poised to become the largest neocloud on the planet, and has set some extremely aggressive goals for itself.

The company will end this year with up to 3 gigawatts of compute capacity, and plans to add around 10 gigawatts more in 2027. Meanwhile, CEO Elon Musk has said his moonshot goal is to bring on 20 gigawatts of additional capacity next year.

SpaceX is currently getting great rates on the compute power it's leasing out, with a payback period of around one year. With a gigawatt of computing power built on Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform costing around $50 billion, that implies the company is getting at least that much in revenue per gigawatt per year. This also lines up with Musk saying SpaceX could end 2027 with annual recurring revenue (ARR) of between $500 billion and $1 trillion.

If SpaceX were to add 10 gigawatts of new compute capacity each year, its "super intelligence" segment (formerly known as its AI segment) would end 2030 with annual recurring revenue of more than $2 trillion. However, it would need to raise capital to fund its capex spending, which I assume will start with 10% dilution and go down 1% a year thereafter. Actual results would vary based on its cost, capex needs, and share price.

Below is a potential scenario as to what SpaceX's AI build-out could potentially look like.

Figures based on aggressive assumptions by author.

Between its AI infrastructure business and the growth of Starlink, Cursor, and its rocket launch business, SpaceX could generate $2 trillion in revenue in 2030. If you speculate that the market will value the company at a forward price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 5 -- a multiple at which Musk's other public company, Tesla, has often traded -- the stock would be worth around $570 by the end of 2029. That would be a more than 300% increase in the stock's price in three years.

The biggest risk to the company hitting this revenue target, meanwhile, would be if compute rental prices fell as it brought more capacity online.

#3129. Prediction: This Is How Much XRP Will Be Worth by the End of 2030

It's time for investors to ratchet down their future growth expectations for XRP.

Future price targets for cryptocurrency XRP (XRP -8.39%) tend to be wildly bullish. Even though XRP is currently trading for just over $1, it's not uncommon to see price targets as high as $100. And, until recently, crypto bulls were convinced that XRP was heading to $1,000.

Unfortunately, XRP has consistently overpromised and under-delivered. In more than a decade of trading, XRP has never traded higher than $3.84.

XRP still has a chance to move higher over the next few years, but investors need to ratchet down their expectations. I predict XRP will only reach $2 by the end of 2030.

On the surface, a price target of $2 might sound underwhelming. After all, XRP traded as high as $3.65 last summer before eventually hitting a brick wall. Earlier in 2025, XRP hit $3.40 before giving back those gains.

But just think of the phenomenal growth rate XRP will need to regain the $4 price level over the next few years. To move from its current price of $1 to a future price of $4, XRP will need to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 40%.

To put that number into context, Bitcoin has delivered a 37% CAGR over the past decade, while Ethereum has delivered a 23% CAGR. So investors are asking XRP to grow faster than either Bitcoin or Ethereum, the two market leaders.

With that in mind, a more realistic growth rate for XRP may be 20%. That's still faster than the growth rate of many established tech companies. If XRP grows at a 20% CAGR over the next four years, it will double in value to $2 by the end of 2030.

Of course, it will take a lot for XRP to achieve a 20% growth rate. First and foremost, new use cases need to be found for the XRP token, which is primarily used now as a bridge currency for cross-border transactions. One of the most interesting new use cases could be real-world asset (RWA) tokenization on the XRP blockchain ledger.

Secondly, the regulatory environment for crypto needs to remain supportive, and new crypto legislation needs to be passed to make it easier for financial institutions and banks to embrace blockchain-based payment technology. It looked like this crypto legislation would pass this year, but the Clarity Act fizzled in the Senate in September.

If both catalysts deliver as planned, XRP could finally see a breakout. But keep your expectations in check. XRP is not going to hit $10, $100, or $1,000. Instead, XRP will be fortunate to double in value and reach $2 by the end of 2030.

#3127. 2027 Tax Brackets and Federal Income Tax Rates

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Each year, the IRS adjusts tax brackets to keep pace with inflation. The 2027 tax brackets were announced on Nov. 5, 2026.

The IRS has released updated tax brackets for 2027, which apply to the taxes we file in 2028. You may notice that the seven tax rates generally stay the same year-to-year — so why do tax brackets get adjusted?

Well, due to inflation, our money might not stretch as far as it did the previous year. To combat that, the IRS adjusts tax brackets so taxpayers can keep a little bit more of their money in a lower tax bracket compared with the previous year.

For example, a single filer could make up to $50,400 in 2026 and pay a top tax rate of 12%. But in 2027, they could make up to $52,025 and still only pay a top tax rate of 12% thanks to these inflation adjustments.

Not sure how to read the tax bracket tables below?

Find your total taxable income in the "tax bracket" column. The corresponding tax rate is the highest rate you'll pay — it doesn’t apply to all your income; it applies only to the portion that falls within that bracket. The income in the lower brackets is taxed at those lower rates.

For example, let's say you’re a single filer and you expect to earn $150,000 this year. The top rate you’d pay on a portion of your income is 24%. The rest would be taxed at 10%, 12% and 22%.

#3124. IRS Announces 2027 Income Tax Brackets, Updated Standard Deduction

Here's a rundown of changes to some well-known tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

Each year, the IRS updates common tax provisions, such as income tax brackets and the standard deduction, to ensure the tax code is keeping pace with the rising cost of living.

These tweaks — formally known as inflation adjustments — help prevent “bracket creep,” where taxpayers who received a cost-of-living raise can pay more in taxes even though their purchasing power remains unchanged.

Inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year were set at 3.2% — larger than the previous two years as inflation heated up. This could mean lower tax bills for some people when they file in 2028.

In the U.S., there are seven marginal rates — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37% — which will remain unchanged for 2027.

Contrary to a popular myth, it’s uncommon for people to pay a single flat federal tax rate on their taxable income. Instead, portions of a person’s income can be taxed at different rates depending on which tax brackets they fall into. For example, some of a person’s income could be taxed at 10%, another chunk at 12%, and so on.

For 2027, the IRS is adjusting those tax brackets — the windows of income that dictate where a tax rate ends and begins — for each filing status. The adjustments mean that some people may be able to keep some of their income in lower tax brackets, and those who received a cost-of-living raise may avoid getting a portion of their income pushed into a higher bracket.

Married filers, for example, can make up to $104,050 to remain with a top tax rate of 12%, compared with $100,800 in 2026. This increase could allow some couples to shelter an additional $3,250 from a higher tax rate in 2027.

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Single filers

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Heads of household

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Married filing separately

» MORE: See the full 2027 tax brackets for each filing status

The IRS lets most filers lower their taxable income by taking the standard deduction or itemizing their returns. The standard deduction, a flat amount based on filing status and age, is popular, as it requires less work to claim and is often more beneficial for those who might not have deductible expenses.

For 2027, the standard deduction will be $16,600 for single filers and those married filing separately, a $500 increase from 2026. Joint filers will be eligible to take $33,200 and heads of household can take $24,925, a $1,000 and $775 increase over 2026, respectively.

» Need help deciding whether to itemize or take the standard deduction? Learn about the differences

Also included in the IRS' 32-page inflation release are various updates to several tax provisions beyond the federal tax brackets. Plus, a brand-new tax credit will go into effect in 2027.

Starting in 2027, taxpayers who contribute to a health flexible spending account (FSA) can contribute up to $3,500 and, if their plan permits, carry over up to $700 into the next tax year.

For those with health savings accounts, the 2027 limit for contributions will rise to $4,500 for self-only coverage and $9,000 for family coverage.

The annual exclusion for gifts, which limits how much taxpayers can give an individual without filing a gift tax return on certain gifts, will be $20,000 per person in 2027, an increase of $1,000 compared with 2026.

The lifetime estate tax exclusion establishes a threshold for the taxation of estates upon a person's death. In 2027, estates valued at or below $15.48 million will not be subject to estate tax, up from $15 million in 2026.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit will launch on Jan. 1. According to the IRS, it aims to support private contributions for K-12 scholarships. Taxpayers who donate to a "scholarship granting organization" in one of the 30 participating states can receive a nonrefundable tax credit of up to $1,700 ($3,400 for couples filing jointly).

#3123. Micron Technology vs. Western Digital: Which Tech Stock Is the Better Buy for 2027?

Both memory and storage stocks are riding the AI data boom, but one may be much better prepared for the next downturn.

The data-heavy world of artificial intelligence (AI) creates massive demand for storage and memory. This shift forces investors to choose between Micron Technology (MU -17.46%) and Western Digital (WDC -17.36%) as they eye long-term gains.

Micron specializes in DRAM and NAND memory used in everything from mobile phones to high-end servers. Western Digital focuses on hard disk drives and flash solutions, specifically targeting the cloud infrastructure sector. Both are booming right now, but the better buy may depend on which business holds up when the boom cools.

As one of the leading semiconductor stocks, Micron Technology designs and manufactures essential memory chips like DRAM and NAND. It serves a wide range of markets including data centers, mobile devices, and the automotive sector. In fiscal 2026 (which ended in September), over half of total revenue came from its top 10 customers, and such customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

Fiscal 2026 revenue reached $133 billion, representing massive year-over-year growth of approximately 256%. Net income grew 895% to $85 billion. This reflects a significant increase from its performance in recent years as memory prices soared due to limited supply and high demand.

As for financial health, the company has virtually no debt. Its current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term obligations with current assets, sits at a healthy 3.3x. Micron also generated nearly $59 billion in free cash flow, which is the cash left over after paying for its operations and capital equipment.

Western Digital provides storage solutions for enterprise clients and hyperscale cloud providers. The cloud end market is vital for the company, accounting for nearly 89% of net revenue in its latest fiscal year.

Trailing-12-month (TTM) revenue through the October quarter reached $14.5 billion, representing growth of 43% over the previous year. Net income reached $10 billion. Western Digital is benefiting from the same dynamic as Micron, with limited supply of storage products driving a favorable pricing environment.

Western Digital has a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.1x. The company holds a current ratio of nearly 1.4x and generated approximately $4.3 billion in free cash flow over the past year.

Both companies face risks from the extreme price volatility often found in the memory and data storage market. These stocks could also fall if anything slowed data center construction, such as new regulations or other restrictions, or if AI infrastructure spending slowed.

Micron competes against major rivals like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Additionally, geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions involving China could limit the company's ability to sell to key infrastructure operators. Western Digital competes against Seagate and Toshiba in the storage market.

Micron trades at a lower Forward P/E, measuring price against future earnings estimates, and a lower P/S ratio, comparing its share price to revenue over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

The better buy is not the stock with the highest upside, but the one that will be more resilient during the next downturn. Western Digital is better positioned to handle a stall in data center spending, and it's the stock I would buy right now.

Micron has seen its revenue and margins soar over the last year, but that sharp swing in its results also shows how vulnerable it is to a sudden dip in memory prices. While it is signing long-term customer agreements to help smooth out future cycles, it won't cover all of its revenue. It is still vulnerable to a downturn in the memory market.

Western Digital is exposed to similar booms and busts as Micron. However, demand for storage products tends to be more stable than memory. This is because data centers will continue to accumulate more data even as spending on new server orders slows.

This is evident in each company's past gross margin. Over the last 10 years, Micron's gross margin has swung from negative 9% in fiscal 2023 to as high as 81% in fiscal 2026. Western Digital's lowest gross margin over the same period was 22% in fiscal 2023, and its highest was 49% in fiscal 2026.

Western Digital's greater resilience is also why the stock trades at a higher P/E. Investors are paying a lower P/E multiple for Micron because they expect greater volatility in its financial results if memory prices fall.

At this point in the cycle, I would rather buy Western Digital heading into 2027.

John Ballard has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology and Western Digital. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3121. CoreCivic (CXW) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Facility sales funded debt cuts and a $500 million buyback, reshaping the balance sheet.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

CoreCivic, Inc. (CXW -7.50%) reported third quarter 2026 financial results highlighted by the execution of strategic real estate divestitures and a significant reduction in corporate debt. Management reported that the company completed the sale of four detention facilities to the federal government for gross proceeds of $2.2 billion, utilizing the net proceeds to retire over $700 million in indebtedness and launch a $500 million accelerated share repurchase program. The company reported that adjusted diluted earnings per share increased 104% compared to the prior year quarter, supported by an occupancy rate of 84% in the residential segment and the contribution of Clinical Solutions Pharmacy. Management indicated that ICE populations nationwide have approached record levels in the second half of 2026, while the company continues to maintain 5,500 beds of idle capacity for future government needs.

The federal government determined the fair market value of these properties by engaging independent appraisers who follow the government mandated yellow book standards as required by federal statute. These rigorous standards direct appraisers to base value on replacement cost under provisions specifically designed to determine a fair market value for special purpose highly improved properties.

This methodology incorporates a variety of relevant factors, including design, condition, age, location, size, available land, and expansion capacity. In addition to the facility sales completed to date, we have been in discussions with ICE about the potential acquisition of additional detention facilities from us.

These discussions are in preliminary stages and we can provide no assurance that any additional sales will occur. Our updated guidance does not include the impact of any potential additional facility sales. We plan to spend $65 million to $75 million on maintenance capital expenditures during 2026 and $12 million for other capital expenditures down $3 million from our prior guidance. Our 2026 forecast also includes $35 million to $40 million for capital expenditures associated with previously idled facilities we are activating and for additional potential facility activations, unchanged from our prior guidance.

We expect adjusted funds from operations or AFFO which we consider a proxy for our cash flow available for capital allocation decisions such as share repurchases and growth CapEx such as acquisitions and facility activations, to range from $260.3 million to $272.3 million for 2026. Although we do not expect to need any meaningful capital expenditures to activate additional idle facilities in 2027, we currently expect some incremental capital expenditures in 2027 to expand the distribution capability of CSP to meet growing market demands for our pharmaceutical services and incremental technology investments to implement opportunities to streamline operations and improve outcomes for residents in our care.

The earn out payment for CSP will also be due next year which we currently estimate to be $29.5 million. We are currently preparing our 2027 budget and expect to provide full year 2027 guidance in connection with our fourth quarter earnings release in February including further detail on our capital expenditures in 2027. That guidance will also reflect estimated financial impact of the change in ownership of the facilities we have sold which may be known by then. #3118. Should You Buy Nvidia Stock Before Nov. 17?

The AI chip maker is trading at a discount.

It has been a challenging month for big tech stocks, including the biggest, Nvidia (NVDA -9.26%).

The world's most valuable company has seen its stock price plummet about 15% since Oct. 6, down to $203 per share as of Nov. 4.

With the artificial intelligence (AI) chip maker set to release third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17, is Nvidia stock a buy at a discount?

Nvidia is the leading provider of graphics processing unit (GPU) chips for data centers and AI computing with a market share of about 75% to 80%.

But Nvidia stock, which has averaged a 65% annualized return over the past three years, has sputtered over the past year. It is up just 9% year to date and over the last 12 months it is up just 2%, trading at $203 per share.

Its struggles mainly stem from continuing concerns over capital expenditures on AI infrastructure by hyperscalers. Will it deliver ROI, or will it just be a drain on earnings and cash flows?

Nvidia is one of the major beneficiaries of that spending, so if these hyperscalers scale back for any reason, might the pullback hurt Nvidia?

Also, Nvidia stock tends to move in tandem with the broader tech sector, which has been trending lower over the past month over these concerns, among others, like high valuations.

But there are other reasons for Nvidia's sluggishness. Some analysts and investors have expressed concern over its so-called "circular financing," with Nvidia investing in companies to have them become its customers.

In addition, its market share, though still high, has dropped from a high of 87% in 2024. Some are also worried that its share could erode further with more competitors, including hyperscalers themselves, making their own chips.

Nvidia has also projected its gross margin to decrease in Q3 to 71% to 72%, down from 75% in Q2. This is due to price increases for its memory components. But the company expects a rebound in fiscal 2028.

Furthermore, the Nov. 3 election brought Democratic control of the House and Senate, and that brings greater uncertainties around the landscape for AI and data center development.

So, with Nvidia's Q3 earnings just two weeks away on Nov. 17, is Nvidia stock a buy?

The fact remains, Nvidia continues to generate huge revenue. In the last quarter, revenue rose 106% year over year to $96.2 billion while AI data center revenue surged 117% to $89 billion. Revenue is anticipated to hit $108 billion in Q3, which would be up 131% from $46.7 billion in Q3 the previous year.

Further, spending on AI by the five hyperscalers is expected to increase to $1.3 trillion in 2027, up from $800 billion in 2026. This is due to a backlog for cloud computing that is over $2 trillion.

The recent sell-off has brought Nvidia stock down, and it's trading at just 25 times earnings and 13 times forward earnings. Any opportunity to get shares of Nvidia at its current low valuation is hard to pass up.

#3116. Rocket Lab Stock Has Lost About 70% From Its Record. Is It Finally a Buy?

Thursday's drop sent the space stock even lower. Is it cheap enough to buy before Monday's report?

Rocket Lab (RKLB -12.18%) stock had another tough day on Thursday. Shares dropped as much as 16% in the session and were roughly $46 as of this writing, while much of the tech sector sold off with them. The space stock closed at a record high of $150.23 on May 27, so it's now about 70% below its peak.

When I last covered Rocket Lab in late October, shares were near $58, and I wasn't willing to buy the growth stock there. The stock's now about 20% cheaper, and the company reports third-quarter results after the close on Monday, Nov. 9.

Is the stock finally a buy at this level?

Including the preferred stock that converts into common shares, Rocket Lab is now worth about $31 billion. Management forecast third-quarter revenue of $250 million to $265 million, which would be 61% to 71% above the $155 million it pulled in during the third quarter of 2025.

Annualizing the midpoint of that range, the stock trades at around 30 times sales. At $58, it traded at closer to 38 times sales. In other words, every dollar of Rocket Lab's revenue costs investors much less now than it did just a few weeks ago.

And revenue growth hasn't been the issue. Rocket Lab has set a revenue record every quarter of 2026 so far. Sales hit $200 million in the first quarter and then $234 million in the second, up 62% year over year.

Showing how strong demand is, Rocket Lab finished June with a record backlog (the value of signed contracts it hasn't booked as revenue yet) of $2.36 billion. It's more than twice the year-ago figure.

Still, a valuation of 30 times sales assumes years of fast growth. And it arguably assumes lots of success for Neutron, the reusable medium-lift rocket Rocket Lab is developing for satellite constellation launches and national security missions.

In mid-October, Rocket Lab pushed Neutron's first launch to 2027. The company found air pockets between the carbon-fiber layers of a dome for the rocket's first-stage propellant tank, and it's making a replacement. Earlier this year, it had already shifted the debut from early 2026 to late 2026.

Rocket Lab hasn't named a new target date. It plans to pick one after testing that it expects to finish in the first quarter of 2027.

Monday's report likely won't say much about Neutron's timing, other than showing if that testing is on track. Until then, investors have to judge the stock by the business Rocket Lab already runs.

Rocket Lab has made strong progress toward profitability. Its adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) loss fell to $8.8 million in the second quarter of 2026, down from $27.6 million the year before. Over the whole first half of the year, the adjusted EBITDA loss was $20.6 million, compared with $57.5 million in the first half of 2025. Its bottom-line net loss narrowed too, to $49 million in the second quarter from $66 million in the year-ago period. And this progress came even while Neutron development helped drive research and development spending up 25% year over year.

But management's third-quarter forecast calls for an adjusted EBITDA loss of $17 million to $23 million. At the midpoint, the company would lose about as much in one quarter as it did in the entire first half.

Part of the reason is a lower expected gross margin. Management expects its non-GAAP (adjusted) gross margin to fall to between 35% and 37% in the third quarter, down from 41.5% in the second.

Sure, Rocket Lab could come in better than its own range. But even the $17 million end of it would be almost double the second-quarter loss -- when the stock has little room for disappointment.

I think the lower price helps, but it doesn't change what Rocket Lab needs to prove. At around 30 times sales, the stock is closer to a price I'd consider paying than it has been at any point this fall.

But the two questions that matter most aren't settled yet. Neutron still has no launch date, and the loss trend is about to reverse, at least for a quarter. With the report just four days away, waiting for it seems to cost a buyer very little.

If the third-quarter loss comes in close to the better end of guidance and Neutron's testing stays on track, I'd consider a small stake after the report. Until then, I'm happy to wait.

#3115. HSA-eligible health plans in 2027: What to know about tax savings vs. higher deductibles

Healthcare affordability was part of the midterm election cost-of-living debate.

It is uncertain how a new Congress might try to address that pain point. Now, as workers choose their 2027 health insurance coverage, millions face a more immediate decision: whether to pick a plan that lets them contribute to a health savings account, or HSA.

The question is whether an HSA-eligible plan with lower premiums and tax benefits is worth the higher deductible and potential out-of-pocket costs.

One noted advantage of an HSA is its tax benefits.

"You have a triple tax advantage," said Kalei Cadinha-Pua'a, vice chair and CEO of Honolulu-based Cadinha & Co., which ranked No. 21 on this year's CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list.

Employer and employee contributions go into the fund before taxes, earnings in the account aren't taxed while they remain in the HSA, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free.

Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors:

Financial advisors say employees often overlook another potential tax savings. HSA contributions made through an employer's Section 125 cafeteria plan generally aren't subject to Social Security and Medicare taxes.

That can make payroll contributions more tax-efficient than contributing on your own and claiming a deduction later, said certified financial planner and enrolled agent Andy Panko, the founder of Tenon Financial in Metuchen, New Jersey.

Workers should check how their employer processes contributions and ask if they receive the Social Security and Medicare tax break on HSA contributions.

A worker who chooses to contribute to an HSA outside of payroll may be able to deduct eligible contributions on their federal tax return but generally won't get the break on Social Security and Medicare taxes.

HSAs are typically paired with a high-deductible health plan, so consumers generally have to be enrolled in a high-deductible health plan in order to contribute to the HSA.

Such a plan may have lower premiums relative to others available to consumers, but workers can face higher costs on the back end when they need care.

For 2027, the IRS says an HSA-eligible plan must generally have a deductible of at least $1,750 for individual coverage or $3,500 for family coverage. The plan's annual out-of-pocket expenses, excluding premiums, cannot exceed $8,700 for individual coverage or $17,400 for family coverage.

More employers are offering health plans with an HSA option. Across all U.S. health plan sponsors with at least 50 employees, 63% offer a high-deductible plan that qualifies for an HSA, according to a recent Marsh employer survey. More than a third, 37%, of all employees covered by an employer health plan are enrolled in an HSA-eligible plan.

"Employers often offer an HSA plan as a low-cost option, and then because of the higher deductible and the overall cost-sharing structure, these plans are typically costing less for the employer as well as the employee," said Frank Easley, senior vice president of Aon Health Solutions.

An HSA's tax advantages don't by themselves make an HSA-eligible plan the right choice. Workers should consider how the plan's premiums, deductible and out-of-pocket maximum align with expected healthcare needs before enrolling, financial advisors say.

They should also factor in any employer HSA contributions and the cash they have available to pay an unexpected medical bill before they reach their deductible, says Nathan Lochstampfor, CFP, an associate consultant at Harrisburg, Pennsylvania-based Conrad Siegel Investment Advisors, which is ranked No. 45 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 for 2026.

If consumers can't afford to pay the deductible of a high-deductible health plan, it may make sense to choose a plan with higher premiums and lower out-of-pocket costs if they need care, he said.

Lochstampfor recommends clients ask themselves: "If I got in a car accident going home today from work, could I afford that deductible? Or would I be better off maybe paying a little bit of higher premiums until I build up those cash reserves?"

HSA contribution limits for 2027 are $4,500 for individuals and $9,000 for families. People age 55 and older can make a $1,000 catch-up contribution.

You can use an HSA to pay for qualified medical expenses now or later. Any money left in the account generally carries over from year to year, and earnings aren't taxed while they remain in the account. HSA balances can also be invested. As of midyear, 11% of HSA accounts held invested assets, according to Devenir, an HSA investment firm.

Ideally, financial advisors say, you keep some of the balance in cash to cover short-term needs and invest the rest for retirement.

"If you have a long time and you can begin to develop a strategy for savings, it can really work and benefit you in the future when you don't have that earned income to pay for your healthcare needs," Cadinha-Pua'a said.

Some HSA owners pay current medical expenses out of pocket and leave money invested in the account so it can grow tax-free. They can use their HSA funds to reimburse themselves years later for those out-of-pocket expenses. Some conditions apply: It must be a qualified medical expense and incurred after the HSA was established, for example.

That strategy can be smart — but it requires good records.

The IRS wants to make sure expenses aren't double counted. Account holders need to keep records showing that any HSA distributions paid or reimbursed qualified medical expenses weren't also claimed as an itemized deduction.

"Be really honest with yourself," Cadinha-Pua'a said. "Are you a good record keeper?"

She recommends making digital copies of receipts, bills and proof of payment, organizing them in an electronic folder and backing up that folder to the cloud. That can help preserve the documentation if a computer fails or the account holder needs to substantiate a reimbursement years later.

#3113. Blue Origin pushes launch to January 2027 as it races to rebuild damaged launchpad

Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin has delayed a return to flight for its flagship New Glenn rocket to January 2027, later than its earlier target of the end of this year, as it rushes to recover from a major explosion in May.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp told employees in a memo Wednesday that the company's launch timing slipped as a result of delays with reconstructing its Cape Canaveral launchpad, including due to bad weather over the summer.

"This small adjustment doesn't diminish what we've accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead," Limp wrote in the memo, which was viewed by CNBC. "Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it's worth it."

The Financial Times earlier reported the memo. The January 2027 time frame is about 10 days later than Blue Origin's earlier launch target, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because the matter is internal.

The New Glenn explosion in May, which occurred during a hot-fire test, badly damaged Blue Origin's Florida launchpad. The company was slated to deploy 48 satellites for Amazon's Leo internet-from-space service just a few days later.

Since then, the company has moved swiftly to repair the launch facility and reworked its pad configuration. Bezos told Fox News last month that the company was still expecting New Glenn to fly again in December.

Limp said Blue Origin has made great progress on the recovery, but he noted that "rebuilding at this pace hasn't been easy."

"Your collective work on our return to flight has been nothing short of remarkable," Limp wrote. "In just six months, Team Blue has accomplished what many thought would take years."

The mishap was inconveniently timed, as Blue Origin has been working to ramp up its launch cadence in an effort to compete with its chief rival, Elon Musk's SpaceX, for commercial and government customers.

The New Glenn delays have hampered Amazon's Leo constellation buildout, for which it relies on Blue Origin for a portion of its launches. Amazon has turned to other providers, including United Launch Alliance and Arianespace, in the interim, especially as SpaceX has phased out Falcon 9 launches to prioritize testing its enormous Starship rocket.

NASA has also tapped Blue Origin for several contracts in the agency's Artemis return-to-the-moon program, including a lunar lander.

The company announced new investments in its Florida launch facilities last month with the goal of supporting multiple flights per week by the end of the decade.

#3112. Loar Holdings: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Loar's $200 million five-year pipeline and steady bolt-on acquisitions point to growth beyond the current cycle, but fleet aging remains an open question.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Loar Holdings (LOAR +4.69%) raised its full-year 2026 net sales outlook to a range of $669 million to $679 million. The manufacturer of proprietary aerospace and defense components continues to expand operating margins through price discipline and volume growth. This operational momentum offers clear visibility into multiyear earnings growth. Three things management said stand out.

#3110. Voters say the economy drove them to the polls — and blame Trump for their troubles

As President Donald Trump campaigned for the nation's highest office in 2024, he regularly blamed Democrats for the country's economic anxiety.

During campaign stops across the U.S., Trump frequently asked voters if they were better off than they were four years prior. At the time, his message appeared to land: In an election centered on inflation and the cost of living, Trump won every swing state and the nationwide popular vote.

Two years later, voters grappling with those same kitchen-table issues took away much of his party's power in Washington and in states across the country.

Democrats rode a blue wave of historic proportions in Tuesday's midterm election to flip everything from battleground congressional seats to long-held Republican governorships. The Democratic Party will now have control of both the House and Senate, ending the Republican Party's trifecta of power in the federal government.

Nearly nine out of 10 voters in the CNBC Voter Poll said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress. Participants in the poll ranked the economy as the most important issue facing the country during the midterm election, ahead of topics like the state of democracy and immigration. Three out of every four survey participants rated the economy as "poor" or "not so good," compared with just 2% who described it as "excellent."

And perhaps most telling of all: Fewer than one out of every five voters said their family's financial standing was better than it was two years ago.

Much of their dissatisfaction was centered on Trump himself, with about two out of every three voters saying his policies worsened economic conditions in the country.

"It was all about the economy," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "Most Americans are struggling with the high inflation and have been for quite some time, and they're just angry."

Tuesday's election played out against the backdrop of a war with Iran that has been politically unpopular and exacerbated the inflationary pressures facing everyday Americans. The CNBC Voter Poll found nearly three out of every four people said the war was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.

Trump told Fox News that voters were presumably unhappy with the surge in gas prices, even if they generally agreed with the need for military action against Iran. Vice President JD Vance said on social media that some voters who backed him and Trump in 2024 likely supported Democrats in the midterms as a result of the war.

U.S. drivers paid about $4.15 for an average gallon of gas on Tuesday, the highest of any midterm or presidential election day since at least 2000, according to AAA. Gas prices have surged about 37% over the past year as the Middle East conflict crippled the global crude trade.

"America sent a very clear message," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, a fuel price tracking platform. "Going into an election with prices that on Election Day have never been higher is something that garners a lot of frustration from consumers."

Higher prices for gas and other energy products have cost the average American household nearly $1,230 since the start of the Iran war, according to an analysis from Zandi. The financial pain felt by U.S. consumers from the conflict has spilled into other areas. Rising borrowing costs and expanded military services roughly cost households more than $900 in addition, according to Zandi.

The consumer price index, a broad basket of goods and services tracked by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, reaccelerated during the war with Iran. Increases in consumer prices have outpaced wage gains in recent months, leaving consumers with less purchasing power.

Prices for diesel, the fuel type used by truckers and trains, climbed to records that transportation executives have said feel "like science fiction." In the latest producer price index report, the BLS said that rising diesel costs pushed up prices for many goods.

The CNBC Voter Poll found more than three out of every five people believed that Trump's policies led to higher prices. Almost nine out of 10 said they were very or somewhat concerned about the prices for a variety of goods such as utilities, food and oil. The poll was a collaborative effort across several news organizations that drew on about 100,000 interviews conducted by phone, online and in-person at polling locations with a margin of error of 0.6%.

Trump took over an economy coming out of the pandemic that was caught in a "vibecession," the term used to describe the disconnect between sour consumer confidence and positive economic fundamentals. With consumer prices now on one of their longest streaks of higher-than-preferred inflation readings on record, the average American's economic sentiment is even worse today.

The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey in 2026 fell to the worst levels in its seven-decade history. The Conference Board, meanwhile, said its consumer confidence gauge in September slid to 14-year lows.

Inflation pushed voters to a "breaking point," said Francesco D'Acunto, a Georgetown University professor who researches behavioral economics. "If consumers become angry voters, they vote against the status quo — in this case, the Trump administration."

Before the U.S. began its war with Iran in late February, economists and monetary policymakers were already sounding the alarm about what Trump's policies could mean for the economy.

Trump pitched his plan for broad and steep tariffs as a way to revive domestic manufacturing, but the policy sent financial markets reeling and raised the prospect of a potential recession. Researchers at the New York Federal Reserve said that several consumer prices would have fallen if not for Trump's tariffs, many of which were later struck down by the Supreme Court.

In the CNBC Voter Poll, 64% said Trump's tariff policies hurt the economy in their area. Just 14% said they helped.

Trump's White House also oversaw mass deportations in major cities that gave way to large-scale protests and the death of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration agents. A University of Pennsylvania study found that the cities experiencing immigration enforcement surges collectively saw decreasing foot traffic and billions of dollars in lost consumer spending.

About three out of five voters said they disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement handled its job and that the Trump administration had gone too far on the issue, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. Still, voters were more likely to say the Republican Party was better at handling immigration.

To be sure, some policies under Trump's White House have been better received. The Internal Revenue Service said in October that the average tax refund grew by 11% following the passage of Trump's "big beautiful bill." So-called Trump Accounts are allowing parents to tap into government and donor funds to build nest eggs for children.

But on Tuesday, voters showed that affordability remained a leading concern as the Iran war continues and inflation pinches pocketbooks. What changed compared with the 2024 presidential election was who they believed could fix it.

In 2024, more voters said they thought Trump was better equipped to handle the economy than former Vice President Kamala Harris. This week, voters said Democrats were better suited than Republicans to manage the economy.

But the party will have a lot of work to do. Seven out of 10 respondents in the CNBC Voter Poll said they felt the U.S. economic system generally favored the wealthy.

"We know pretty clearly what is making Americans upset," said Zandi, who has advised politicians from both parties. "There's another election coming up in two years. Hopefully, policymakers are listening to all this."

#3108. Zoetis: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Zoetis (ZTS -7.95%) reported a 1% revenue decline, excluding currency and acquisition effects. Lower veterinary clinic visits and generic competition continue to pressure pet care returns. Three things management said stand out.

The long-term thesis depends on converting lifecycle line extensions into durable market share while commercializing new therapeutic categories across renal disease, cardiology, and oncology.

#3107. What Wall Street billionaires are saying about Democrats' midterm sweep

America's billionaires woke up Wednesday to a political reckoning — and a Wall Street rally.

As Democrats celebrated a sweeping midterm victory, some of the country's wealthiest donors traded barbs over record election spending. Others warned the results could threaten the artificial intelligence boom.

Wall Street, however, cheered the outcome. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%, as investors welcomed political gridlock, reduced uncertainty and President Donald Trump's willingness to accept the results.

Virgin Group founder Richard Branson took aim at the billions spent influencing the election.

"I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent," Branson wrote Wednesday on LinkedIn, calling for campaign finance reform. Branson did not give donations that met the reporting threshold in the 2026 election cycle.

His comments came as Elon Musk, the election's largest individual donor, watched his preferred Republicans lose the Texas Senate and governor races despite pouring $224 million into the state — nearly half his record $474 million in political giving nationwide, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records.

Early Wednesday, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO suggested on X that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing before joking that his "election-interfering space lasers" had failed.

LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, another major political donor, took a sharper tone.

"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote late Tuesday on X, accusing Musk of spending "outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power" while defending his own contributions to Democrats.

Other Democratic megadonors celebrated. "The world changed yesterday," Alex Soros wrote Wednesday on X, hailing the results as a generational victory after his family contributed roughly $103 million to Democratic political efforts.

But beyond the political sparring, some of the country's richest investors were focused on a potentially bigger consequence of the Democratic sweep: the future of the AI boom.

Even before polls closed Tuesday, Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that slowing AI development could jeopardize America's technological edge. "Practically speaking, we can't slow down," he said.

As results rolled in Tuesday night, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya sounded an even starker warning.

Palihapitiya initially questioned whether the early results would hold, but warned that if they did, the implications for the AI trade could be severe.

"And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers," Palihapitiya said during an election night livestream of the "All-In" podcast.

Texas offered an early test of those fears. Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has proposed a moratorium on new data center construction until stronger safeguards are established, defeated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.

During the same livestream, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner warned the Democratic wave could mean at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI data center capacity would not come online in 2027. Wall Street analyst Dan Ives estimated Wednesday that 10% of planned U.S. data centers would no longer go ahead.

Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su acknowledged the growing resistance to AI's expansion, urging technology companies to demonstrate the benefits of data centers to local communities.

"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," Su told CNBC on Wednesday.

Yet Wall Street may have found opportunity in the same slowdown that worried AI's biggest backers.

Fewer new data centers could increase the value of existing facilities while easing the enormous spending burden on technology giants. Big Tech stocks surged Wednesday, adding more than $750 billion in market value at one point, even as smaller, debt-dependent data center operators tumbled.

#3103. California’s billionaire tax faces defeat, but Democrats plan higher taxes on the wealthy

A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

The likely defeat of the California billionaire tax may energize Democrats in Congress to propose federal tax hikes on high earners along with a potential federal wealth tax, according to tax experts.

While the votes in California are still being counted, 56% of the state's voters have voted "no" on the billionaire tax while 44% voted "yes." The ballot measure requires a majority of votes for approval, so election experts say a defeat is likely. The tax, known as Proposition 40, would have imposed a one-time levy of 5% on the net worth of Californians worth over $1 billion.

Two ballot measures designed as poison pills against the billionaire tax are garnering strong support. Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, which limit revenue use and prevent any state taxation of personal assets, are both showing majority "yes" votes. If either gets more votes than the billionaire tax, the billionaire tax is defeated.

Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the healthcare union that sponsored the billionaire tax proposal, all but conceded defeat Tuesday night, saying they will try again in 2028 unless the legislature takes action to "make billionaires pay their fair share."

Proposals to raise income taxes on the wealthy fared better in other states. In Washington State, voters supported a new "millionaire tax," which would impose a 9.9% tax rate on household income of more than $1 million a year. In Colorado, the passage of a plan to replace the flat tax of 4.4% with a graduated income tax with a top rate of 8.4% on income over $1 million, is too close to call.

With Democrats now set to control both the House and the Senate, tax experts expect a flurry of new tax proposals aimed at raising taxes on high earners to cut taxes for lower- and middle-income taxpayers.

"It is clear Democrats will try to lower taxes for middle-income households and raise taxes on certain businesses and high-income households," said Howard Gleckman, nonresident fellow at the Tax Policy Center. "But it is much too soon to know how."

The proposals could include plans like those floated last year by Senators Chris Van Hollen, D-Md, and Cory Booker, D-N.J. Van Hollen's plan calls for a new graduated surtax on those earning more than $1 million, starting with a 5% surtax for those making between $1 to $2 million and rising to 12% for those earning more than $5 million a year. The new top rate would be 49% under the existing 37% top marginal rate.

The hikes would be offset by a tax cut on middle- and lower-income taxpayers, creating a new exemption equal to $46,000 for single filers and $92,000 for joint filers. Van Hollen has also proposed increasing the capital gains top tax rate from 23.8% to 35.8%.

Booker's plan is similar, but would increase the top rate to 43% and more than double the standard deduction to $37,500 for single filers and $75,000 for joint filers.

While taxing the wealthy has proven popular among Democrats, pairing the tax hikes with tax cuts for lower or middle-income taxpayers could prove challenging given the deficits, tax experts say.

"A key question is the debate about how much to prioritize further cuts at all, given the revenue needs for the deficit situation and the Democrats' spending priorities," said Garrett Watson, vice president of federal tax policy at the Tax Foundation. He said those priorities include reversing Trump-era tax cuts as well as expanding spending.

Plans for a federal wealth tax or tax on unrealized gains could also get more attention. Congressman Ro Khanna, D-Calif., who campaigned for the California billionaire tax and whose Silicon Valley district is home to substantial tech wealth, teamed up with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt, on what they call the "Make Billionaires Pay Their Fair Share Act."

The plan would impose a 5% tax on total net worth of those worth more than $1 billion. Yet unlike California's tax, which was a one-time levy, the Khanna-Sanders plan would be an annual tax.

Of course, President Trump would likely veto any Democratic tax plan, especially if it takes aim at the Trump tax cuts passed in 2017 and extended and expanded last year. But tax experts say any Democratic plans introduced in the next two years could influence tax policy in the 2028 election and highlight the party's priorities.

"Proposals made in 2027 will shape the direction of policy in the future," the Tax Foundation said in a report. "While their ambitions to raise taxes will be limited by President Trump's veto, these proposals will serve as messaging and discussion vehicles over the next two years on the direction of the tax code."

#3102. The Nasdaq Plunges 5%. What the Data Center Crash Means for Investors

Investors are afraid of a data center slowdown. Will it really happen?

That question was on the minds of millions of investors on Thursday, as the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.52%) had one of its worst days ever, plunging 5.5% as fears spread that a political backlash could choke the AI boom, following the midterm election.

Investors believe that election winners in Texas and elsewhere will slap significant restrictions or even outright bans on data centers, which became a lightning rod during the campaign. After chip stocks were among the few losers on Wednesday, they collapsed on Thursday, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF losing 11.2%. Even industry leader Nvidia lost 9.1%, and the crash triggered a broader sell-off across the stock market, with all 11 sectors falling, even defensive ones like utilities and consumer staples.

AI infrastructure stocks began to wobble a few weeks ago, starting with a chart showing that neocloud operator CoreWeave's (CRWV -9.83%) bond yields had risen as high as 15%, and worries about a potential default sent the stock tumbling.

Earnings reports from the big hyperscalers were greeted similarly, as investors worried about soaring capital expenditures and negative free cash flow, even as these companies continue to grow rapidly and are hugely profitable.

Then, the election happened, and now fears of a slowdown in the data center build-out have led investors to flee AI stocks.

Stock market reactions to elections are famously rash and often fleeting. Stocks tumbled following the Brexit decision before bouncing back over the following days, and stocks plunged overnight when President Trump was first elected before turning green the following day.

This looks like a similar reaction. Tech stocks initially fell on Tuesday night before the Nasdaq jumped on Wednesday. The response is understandable as data centers have been a major talking point during the campaign, but the sell-off seems like an overreaction.

Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, campaigned on a temporary moratorium on data centers and reasonable guidelines, like a ban on subsidies for data centers. However, she is no radical, telling CNN, "We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections."

In a worst-case scenario with a significant slowdown in data center construction in the U.S., most industry observers believe that activity would just move abroad, meaning that industry growth wouldn't be significantly impacted.

In an interview with the Motley Fool, Arm Holdings (ARM -13.08%) CFO Jason Child explained his thinking on the matter, saying, "Let's just say it (the data centers) all slows down. Do we believe AI demand will slow down? I think, generally, most people say no. The genie is out of the bottle." Child also said he was generally skeptical of any political reaction and said the bipartisan interest in economic growth was too strong for there to be a significant slowdown in the build-out. He also noted that Arm could still benefit from a slowdown in data center construction, as Arm's chips excel at performance per watt, which would be in greater demand if data center construction were artificially limited.

Predicting where the data center debate goes from here isn't easy, but Child is right that demand for AI is strong and is unlikely to be shaken by any slowdown in capacity growth.

Meanwhile, many of the top AI stocks are looking cheaper than ever. Nvidia (NVDA -9.26%) now trades at a forward P/E of less than 20, and it's nearly doubling its revenue each quarter. Micron (MU -17.46%), the memory chip leader, is trading at a forward P/E of less than 4.

Many of these AI stocks have already soared this year, so the pullback needs to be seen in that context, but like "Liberation Day" and other political issues that have rocked markets, this response seems likely to be an overreaction and a non-issue within the next year. Buying the dip on quality stocks like Nvidia looks like a smart move.

#3099. HubSpot: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Management is betting on pricing changes and buyer behavior over near-term customer counts, a trade-off that likely defines the next several years.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings conference call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, HubSpot (HUBS -5.39%) reported constant-currency revenue growth of 17% year over year. As artificial intelligence transforms how customer relationship software creates value, understanding how the business adapts pricing and product delivery is critical for shareholders.

HubSpot is adjusting its pricing by combining fixed seat costs with usage-based credits for its artificial intelligence tools. This strategy aims to lower initial pricing barriers for smaller accounts while capturing upside as clients consume more automated services over time.

Macroeconomic pressures and artificial intelligence evaluation criteria are altering client purchasing behavior across market tiers. Larger enterprise accounts require broader executive approval, while smaller businesses are more sensitive to overall software expenditures.

Management is prioritizing long-term platform adoption over short-term net additions, which measure net new customer expansion. A structural reorganization implemented in October reallocates resources toward artificial intelligence capabilities and employee retention.

Artificial intelligence adoption is accelerating across the platform, as evidenced by higher retention and deeper data integration. Leadership is watching pricing discipline and sales execution during this multiyear shift.

Disciplined cost management reinforces multiyear margin targets.

#3097. Time to Cash Out? 4 Energy Stocks I'd Sell Before It's Too Late

If you are watching energy prices rise, remember that they also fall.

There are two things that connect Devon Energy (DVN -2.81%), Diamondback Energy (FANG -1.80%), EOG Resources (EOG -1.48%), and Permian Resources (PR -4.86%), since all four are, one, U.S.-based, and two, energy producers. That's been a very good thing lately, as energy prices have been strong. But history is very clear that energy prices won't stay strong forever. Here's why you may want to sell now to lock in some gains before it's too late.

Energy prices rise and fall over time. There are any number of reasons why energy prices change, from supply and demand dynamics to disasters (manmade and otherwise) to geopolitical conflict. That last one is what's driving prices higher today, with the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East upending global energy markets.

There's been a secondary benefit for U.S. energy producers such as Devon Energy, Diamondback Energy, EOG Resources, and Permian Resources because countries around the world are rethinking energy security. That makes production from an economically and politically stable region like North America extra attractive. So there is reason to be optimistic about these companies over the long term.

However, you can't ignore the key fact here: commodity prices are the main driver of an energy producer's business. The graph below makes that very clear, as you can see that the stocks have been tracking the price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI), a key U.S. energy benchmark (the blue line).

The problem is that oil prices have been moving in line with investor sentiment amid the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East. Energy prices rise when investors think the conflict is worsening; they fall when the outlook for the conflict improves. However, from a big-picture perspective, the conflict is unlikely to last forever. That means that there could be material downside risk in owning pure-play producers like Devon Energy, Diamondback Energy, EOG Resources, and Permian Resources.

With nothing to soften the blow when commodity prices fall, their revenues and earnings will take a hit. And investors won't wait for quarterly earnings to find out how bad it is; they'll start selling as soon as energy prices begin to decline. Or at least, that's what history shows is most likely to happen.

If you have been lucky enough to benefit from the rising tide that's lifting all of the boats in the energy production space, it might be time to take some profits. That's what I would be considering right now, while energy prices remain elevated. The big wild card that would push me to pull the trigger was the midterm elections, which seem likely to lead to a more dovish stance in both the U.S. Congress and the House.

If I'm correct in my assumption here, the conflict will lack the political support it has had up until now. And that could force a resolution that would ultimately lead to lower energy prices.

I own a pipeline company (Enbridge (ENB -1.37%)) and an integrated energy giant (TotalEnergies (TTE -1.89%)) specifically to minimize the impact of volatile energy prices on my energy investments. Buying stocks like Devon Energy, Diamondback Energy, EOG Resources, and Permian Resources is basically going all in on commodity risk. In fact, investors often buy stocks like these specifically to benefit from rising energy prices.

I think you should buy and hold for the long term, which is why I own what I own. However, if you've chosen to buy a pure-play energy producer, you may want to reconsider your commitment given the evolving narrative in the energy sector. That's not a market-timing call; it's just a realistic view of the sector's changing situation. If you still want some energy exposure, you might consider shifting into a high-yield, fee-driven pipeline stock like Enbridge or Enterprise Products Partners (EPD -0.24%).

Reuben Gregg Brewer has positions in Enbridge and TotalEnergies Se. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Enbridge. The Motley Fool recommends EOG Resources and Enterprise Products Partners. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3085. Why Warby Parker Stock Popped Today

The brand's AI-powered Intelligent Eyewear could be a lucrative new growth driver.

Shares of Warby Parker (WRBY +22.50%) soared more than 22% on Thursday after the eyewear maker highlighted the upcoming launch of its new smart glasses.

Warby Parker's revenue rose 10.4% year over year to $244.7 million in the third quarter.

The eyeglass designer opened 12 net new stores during the quarter, bringing its total count to 364 locations as of Sept. 30.

Warby Parker's high-quality yet affordable prescription glasses starting at $95 are proving popular with budget-conscious consumers. The company's strategy of offering vision tests and eye exams in its retail stores is also helping to bring in more customer traffic.

Active customers grew 3% to 2.74 million on a trailing 12-month basis. People are also spending more at Warby Parker's stores. Average revenue per customer increased 6.7% to $342.

"We're continuing to expand our products and services, build on the investments we've made over many years, like exams and insurance, and find new ways to serve our customers," Co-CEO Neil Blumenthal said.

All told, Warby Parker's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) jumped 11% to $28.6 million.

Management now sees full-year net revenue rising as much as 12% to $976 million in 2026, resulting in adjusted EBITDA of roughly $118 million.

Warby Parker is gearing up for the launch of its Intelligent Eyewear, a line of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered smart glasses developed in partnership with Samsung and Alphabet's Google. They offer real-time translation, turn-by-turn navigation, high-quality photo taking, and other voice-activated features.

"One week from today, on November 12, we'll begin accepting pre-orders for our first Intelligent Eyewear collection and look forward to delivering customer orders during the holiday season," Co-CEO Dave Gilboa said. "We can't wait for customers to experience these remarkable products firsthand."

Demand for the acquired energy drink brand Alani Nu propelled overall portfolio results, while core brand sales were affected by retail inventory adjustments. Investors must evaluate whether corporate restructuring and promotional discipline can expand gross profit margins. Three takeaways from the call highlight the company's path forward.

Alani Nu generated net sales of $410 million, up 24% year over year as retail product distribution expanded. That sales momentum cushioned temporary revenue declines in core CELSIUS products while retailers adjusted inventory levels.

Managing distinct beverage lines under one parent company created operational complexity across sales channels. Leadership established brand-led business units to give each beverage line dedicated executive focus while sharing distribution scale.

Elevated costs for aluminum cans and diesel fuel squeezed third-quarter gross margin, the percentage of revenue left after production and freight expenses, down to 46.8%. Management is implementing structured pricing and promotional discipline across retail accounts to lower trade spending and rebuild profitability.

Product innovation and expanded distribution networks drive current commercial momentum. Non-U.S. market revenue rose 56% year over year as brand awareness doubled across European markets. Management is monitoring promotional trade efficiency, direct-store-delivery distribution integration, and aluminum price fluctuations to safeguard long-term returns.

Supply chain integration across acquired brands unlocks structural scale benefits across major retail channels. Operational discipline positions the business to turn retail shelf expansion into sustained cash generation.

#3078. Kimberly-Clark vs. Lululemon Athletica: Which Consumer Goods Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

One trades at a cheaper valuation, while the other boasts stronger cash generation.

One company provides everyday essentials while the other defines premium lifestyle apparel. Deciding between Kimberly-Clark (KMB +1.53%) and Lululemon Athletica (LULU -0.26%) depends on your preference for stability versus growth.

Kimberly-Clark dominates household essentials with brands like Kleenex and Huggies, offering a defensive play for conservative investors. Conversely, Lululemon Athletica leads the high-performance apparel market through an efficient direct-to-consumer model. Both firms are navigating shifting consumer habits, but they offer vastly different risk and reward profiles for investors looking ahead to 2027.

Kimberly-Clark provides essential personal care and tissue products to consumers through brands like Huggies and Kleenex. Its largest customer is Walmart (WMT -1.12%), which accounted for nearly 16% of net sales in its latest annual report filed for the period ending December 31, 2025. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business if purchasing patterns shift.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $16.4 billion, representing a decline of approximately 2.1% compared to the previous year. Despite the lower top-line figure, the company reported net income of roughly $2 billion. Looking more closely at its financial picture, the company has $956 million in total cash and $6.5 billion in total debt. Operating cash flow over the 12-month trailing period is $3.3 billion.

Lululemon designs and sells high-performance athletic apparel through an omni-channel retail model that includes company-operated stores and e-commerce. It operates within the consumer discretionary stocks category, focusing on premium brand positioning. The company also utilizes wholesale channels like fitness studios and athletic organizations to reach specialized audiences.

In FY 2025, revenue reached roughly $11.1 billion, which represents growth of nearly 4.9% over the prior year. The company generated net income of approximately $1.6 billion during this period. Lululemon has $1.3 billion in total cash and $2.1 billion in total debt. Operating cash flow over the 12-month trailing period is $1.9 billion.

Kimberly-Clark faces intense competition from both branded and private-label rivals in the consumer products space. It is also sensitive to price volatility for raw materials like pulp, often sourced from large providers like Suzano (SUZ -0.63%). Additionally, the company must manage risks associated with its Kenvue acquisition, including integration challenges and higher indebtedness.

Lululemon operates in the fiercely competitive athletic apparel market, where it must constantly adapt to changing consumer preferences. The company remains vulnerable to supply chain disruptions, as its production is heavily concentrated. Furthermore, recent changes to trade policies and duty-free exemptions could impact its cost structure.

Lululemon currently trades at a lower multiple on both sales and earnings estimates compared to the more defensive Kimberly-Clark.

Right off the bat, I would pick Kimberly-Clark in this battle. One reason is that 2027 is likely to be as full of investment uncertainty as 2026. But with a more defensive stock like Kimberly-Clark, you have less to worry about in your portfolio. That's because its brands, from Band-Aid to Cottonelle, are products people will always buy, no matter what's going on in the stock market or the economy.

Also, Kimberly-Clark is a Dividend King, which requires the company to have increased its dividend payouts for 50 or more consecutive years. It's cleared that hurdle by boosting its payout for 54 consecutive years, and it's also paid a dividend for 92 consecutive years. Speaking of its dividend, it currently yields 4.6%.

The company can serve as a defensive position within a portfolio, but one thing to watch is its recent acquisition of the consumer health brand Kenvue. On paper, the two seem like they would mix well, but there's always the risk that an acquisition won't work out as smoothly as anticipated.

In comparison, Lululemon is a company working on its next chapter. Its sales are declining, and it brought in a new CEO in September. As it will take some time for changes to be implemented, the company is on less solid footing than Kimberly-Clark.

Jack Delaney has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Walmart. The Motley Fool recommends Lululemon Athletica Inc. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.
