#3077. Brookfield Renew (BEPC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Liquidity and asset recycling fueled a record quarter as nuclear and battery plans expanded.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Brookfield Renewable Corporation (BEPC -0.92%) reported record financial results for the third quarter, supported by high levels of liquidity and a significant expansion in nuclear and battery storage initiatives. Management stated that the company remains on track to achieve a run rate of 10 gigawatts of commissioned capacity by 2027. The company is currently progressing a corporate simplification plan to combine with its partnership entity, though the voting deadline was extended to Nov. 25, 2026 to meet the required approval threshold. Strategic focuses during the period included the closing of major acquisitions, the advancement of a $120 billion nuclear framework agreement, and the execution of a programmatic capital recycling strategy that generates recurring proceeds for reinvestment.

Operator: Hello, and welcome to the Brookfield Renewable. Third Quarter 26 Results Conference Call and Webcast. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press *11 on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising your hand has been raised. To withdraw your question, please press *11 again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce CEO, Connor David Teskey.

Connor David Teskey: Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, thank you for joining us for our third quarter 26 conference call. Before we begin, we would like to remind you that a copy of our news release and investor supplement can be found on our website. We also want to remind you that we may make forward looking statements on this call. These statements are subject to known and unknown risks, and our future results may differ materially. For more information, you are encouraged to review our regulatory filings available on SEDAR+ EDGAR, and on our website.

On today's call, we will review our third quarter results discuss what we are seeing in the energy markets today, highlight the continued execution of our growth initiatives, and outline how we continue to position the business for long term value creation. Patrick will then review our financial results, our balance sheet, and our funding activities including our growing capital recycling program, and he will also provide an update on our proposed simplification. Following our comments, we look forward to taking your questions. Turning first to the quarter, we delivered record financial results and are accelerating our growth activities. We continue to scale our recurring capital recycling program alongside our steadily growing development platform.

Lastly, we are also strengthening our financial position ending the quarter with $5.1 billion of liquidity positioning the business to capitalize on opportunities in the current environment. In the third quarter, we delivered FFO of $346 million or $0.51 per unit. Up 15% year over year or 11% on a per unit basis. In the last 12 months, we delivered FFO of $1.488 billion or $2.18 per unit up 15%, 12%, respectively, compared to the prior year period. We invested or committed $3 billion into growth or $700 million net to BEP during the quarter. Including closing our acquisition of Boralex, a leading global renewable platform.

Subsequent to quarter end, we closed the acquisition of IPA, the largest stand alone battery storage platform in North America, strengthening our battery storage capabilities. We continue to scale our development through the addition of new platforms and the acceleration of organic growth activities across our existing businesses, commissioning 2.5 GW of new capacity in the quarter. We also further derisked our advanced pipeline by signing power purchase agreements for 1.6 GW of additional projects And today, we remain on track to ramp up our run rate of 10 GW of commission capacity by 2027.

Alongside our growing development, we continue to scale our capital recycling program agreeing to or closing sales since the end of the second quarter, that are expected to generate approximately $2.8 billion in proceeds or $850 million net to BEP at strong returns. As demonstrated in recent years, this is a new and consistent earnings driver to our business and the natural result of the increasing amount of new capacity we bring online each quarter from organic growth.

As our business grows, we have an increasingly large and diverse pool of assets available for sale and our flexibility to sell individual assets portfolios, entire platforms, or minority stakes allows us to consistently crystallize value and generate a growing amount of recurring and accretive capital to fund our growth. Before discussing the broader energy market, and providing an update on our growth initiatives, We thought it would be worth highlighting the resilience of our business in an environment of higher interest rates and inflation. We have an incredibly durable platform that has delivered strong results through periods of both lower and higher rates.

For new developments, we underwrite projects based on prevailing interest rates passing financing costs through into contract prices while preserving our target returns. And with substantially all of our existing proportionate debt at fixed rates, our business is well insulated from rising rates. We also benefit from inflation linkage across ~70% of our revenues which when combined with our high margins, provides a positive earnings tailwind during inflationary periods and positions our platform to deliver durable, and growing cash flows over time. Turning to the energy markets, The environment for our business remains highly constructive. Global demand for power continues to grow outpacing new supply. Driven by the long standing trends of electrification re-industrialization and digitalization.

At the same time, governments are increasingly focused on securing reliable and affordable power to support economic growth, and energy independence. This widening supply demand imbalance is driving strong demand for renewable generation alongside investment in battery storage, and nuclear power, to provide the scale and reliability needed to support expanding electricity grids. Against this backdrop, we continue to see significant opportunities to invest in these technologies and deliver differentiated integrated solutions. Importantly, we remain disciplined in how we pursue growth continuing to develop projects backed by long term contracts with some of the largest and most creditworthy buyers of power in the world. During the quarter, we made meaningful progress advancing strategic priorities within our nuclear business Westinghouse.

#3076. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#3075. Palo Alto Networks vs. Zscaler: Which Cybersecurity Stock Is a Better Buy Going Into 2027?

Palo Alto Networks trades at a steep premium to Zscaler on sales and forward earnings, but its platform strategy and 24.5% revenue growth complicate the valuation debate.

Is a platform-based approach or a cloud-native architecture better for securing the digital future? That's the choice for investors between Palo Alto Networks (PANW -9.59%) and Zscaler (ZS -9.16%). Both offer compelling reasons to invest for those seeking exposure to the cybersecurity sector going into 2027.

Palo Alto Networks is transitioning from legacy hardware to an integrated AI-driven security platform for global enterprises. In contrast, Zscaler focuses on its purpose-built zero trust exchange to secure decentralized workforces. They are leaders in a rapidly expanding market, but their financial health and valuation profiles offer distinct paths for everyday investors.

Palo Alto Networks operates as a global provider of AI-driven cybersecurity, securing networks, clouds, and endpoints through its integrated platform. The company serves over 70,000 customers, including major government entities and large enterprises across the financial services and healthcare sectors. Two distributors collectively accounted for 30% of total revenue in fiscal 2026, and customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In its 2026 fiscal year (FY), ended July 31, revenue reached $11.5 billion, which represents growth of 24.5% compared to the prior fiscal year. The company reported net income of $307 million for the period, resulting in a net margin of 2.7%. This profitability level is a notable decrease from the 12.3% net margin recorded during the previous fiscal year.

As of its July 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.1x, which means the company holds very little total debt relative to what shareholders own. The current ratio was 0.9x, measuring its ability to cover short-term liabilities with assets that can be converted to cash within a year. Free cash flow for the year was $4.1 billion, representing cash from operations minus capital expenditures. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 39% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Zscaler provides a cloud-native zero trust platform that connects users and devices directly to authorized applications rather than the entire network. The company serves approximately 11,000 customers globally, including more than 50% of the Fortune 500 and 40% of the Forbes Global 2000. It relies heavily on channel partners for distribution, with its top five partners accounting for roughly 31% of revenue in fiscal 2026.

In FY 2026, ended July 31, Zscaler reported revenue of $3.4 billion, reflecting growth of 25.4% over the previous twelve-month period. The company recorded a net loss of $63.2 million, which resulted in a net margin of negative 1.9%. While the company has not yet reached GAAP profitability, it continues to focus on growing its user base and expanding its partnership with IBM and Red Hat.

According to its July 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.7x. The current ratio was 1.7x, suggesting the company maintains a healthy cushion to meet its short-term financial obligations. Free cash flow reached $852.4 million for the fiscal year ended in July. Note that stock-based compensation represented 72.8% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation.

Palo Alto Networks faces intense competition from established large companies like Microsoft and Alphabet. These rivals increasingly offer native security capabilities that could disadvantage platforms with less integration. The company also manages risks from its acquisition strategy, including the complex integration of businesses like CyberArk and Chronosphere, alongside legal risks from pending patent infringement litigation.

Zscaler has a history of annual net losses and faces the challenge of achieving profitability while competing against legacy vendors and other cloud providers. It is heavily dependent on channel partners who may choose to promote competing products from Fortinet or Check Point Software Technologies. Furthermore, the company manages significant operations in India, where rising wage costs for skilled professionals could impact future operating margins.

Zscaler appears to be the more attractively valued option for investors because it carries significantly lower multiples for both sales and earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The Forward P/E ratio compares the current share price to future earnings estimates. The P/S ratio measures the market capitalization of a company divided by its sales over the past twelve months.

Between cybersecurity stocks Palo Alto Networks and Zscaler, the more compelling choice for 2027 is Palo Alto Networks. It is the larger company that not only produces far greater top-line figures, its fiscal 2026 free cash flow of $4.1 billion towers over Zscaler's $852.4 million, giving it plenty of funds to invest into its business.

Palo Alto Networks is also a profitable enterprise, although its fiscal 2026 net income of $307 million represented a year-over-year drop due to costs associated with its acquisitions, particularly CyberArk. Meanwhile, Zscaler has yet to turn a profit.

Both are pricey stocks, given their elevated forward earnings multiples, which contributed to recent pullbacks in their share prices. However, Palo Alto Networks' "platformization" strategy, where it seeks to consolidate customer cybersecurity spending from multiple vendors onto just its services, is working well. In its fiscal Q4, the company reported a record number of net new platformization customers. As this strategy's success grows, it increases the threat that Zscaler could lose some of its customers to its larger rival.

Robert Izquierdo has positions in Alphabet, International Business Machines, Microsoft, and Palo Alto Networks. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Check Point Software Technologies, Fortinet, International Business Machines, Microsoft, and Zscaler. The Motley Fool recommends Palo Alto Networks. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3074. Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Jeffrey Epstein when they take Senate control

Senate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan Chase's banking relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once they take control of Congress early next year.

Democratic staffers on the Senate Finance Committee intend to home in on how high-ranking executives at JPMorgan handled Epstein, a source familiar with the panel's thinking told CNBC on Thursday. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the probe of the nation's biggest bank has not been announced.

The Finance Committee is likely to be chaired beginning in January by Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who currently is the panel's ranking member. Wyden has made clear he plans to make full use of the subpoena powers that committee majorities wield.

Democratic staffers aim to focus in particular on decisions about Epstein made by Mary Callahan Erdoes, the CEO of JPMorgan's asset and wealth management division, the source said.

JPMorgan declined to comment. The bank has previously said it regrets any association with Epstein but that it did not assist him in committing crimes.

In a 2023 deposition, Erdoes said she was aware as early as 2006 that Epstein was accused of paying cash to have underage girls brought to his home. Epstein had been a client of the bank since 1998.

Epstein became a registered sex offender after pleading guilty in 2008 in Florida to a state criminal charge of procuring an underage girl for prostitution.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon in his own, later deposition in 2023, said Erdoes had authority to cut off Epstein as a client. She did not take that step until 2013.

Epstein, a former friend of President Donald Trump, ex-President Bill Clinton and many other high-profile people, died in a jailhouse suicide in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on federal child sex trafficking charges.

A lawyer for the U.S. Virgin Islands told a federal judge in New York in 2023 that JPMorgan "was a full-service bank for Jeffrey Epstein's sex trafficking," and that it waited until after he killed himself to notify the Treasury Department of $1 billion in suspicious transactions related to trafficking by Epstein.

"This was a CYA [cover your a--] reporting after 16 years of all of the monies flowing in his JPMorgan accounts after he was dead," the lawyer, Mimi Liu, said.

JPMorgan has blamed former investment banking chief Jes Staley for concealing or failing to report criminal activity related to Epstein, with whom he had a close relationship.

Staley, who left JPMorgan in 2013 and later became CEO of Barclays before stepping down in 2021, has denied knowledge of Epstein's crimes.

House Oversight Chair James Comer, R-Ky., after a closed-door interview with Staley in July, said that the former executive had encouraged JPMorgan to keep Epstein as a client.

In mid-2023, JPMorgan agreed to a $290 million settlement with victims of Epstein without admitting wrongdoing. That same year, JPMorgan agreed to pay $75 million to settle a separate lawsuit by the U.S. Virgin Islands alleging that the bank facilitated and benefited from the sex trafficking of young women by Epstein.

In August, Wyden released a report accusing top officials at multiple banks of "looking the other way" as Epstein moved hundreds of millions of dollars to finance a yearslong sex trafficking operation.

"The report exposes how top bankers shielded Epstein from federal scrutiny by delaying the reporting of Epstein's suspicious financial activity to the U.S. government, likely in violation of federal anti-money-laundering laws," Wyden's office said in a statement that month.

"It includes new details about the extent of suspicious activity reported by Deutsche Bank after Epstein's death, new details from bank reports filed about suspicious transfers to Epstein through accounts at Bank of America, and names top officials at JPMorgan Chase and other banks who were responsible for reporting Epstein's shady activities to the government but instead protected Epstein in order to gain access to Leon Black and other billionaires."

Black, former CEO of Apollo Global Management, was revealed to have paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice in the years after his 2008 conviction.

In September, Black sued the House oversight panel, seeking to block subpoenas it had issued him for his testimony and for documents related to its Epstein probe.

On Wednesday, Black sued Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to become chair of the Oversight Committee in the next Congress, alleging Garcia defamed him in statements regarding Epstein. The lawsuit focuses on Garcia's claims in a TV interview that Black "is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein's crimes" and "was one of the last people to actually interact" with Epstein before his death, among others.

The Department of Justice's mountain of files related to Epstein became a major focus in late 2025 and early 2026, after Congress passed a bill ordering the DOJ to make those records public.

Trump's name is referenced thousands of times in the files that have been released.

The president has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, with whom he fell out in the early 2000s.

#3071. Chipotle Mexican Grill vs. e.l.f. Beauty: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy?

Comparing Chipotle to e.l.f. reveals vastly different risk-reward profiles.

Investors choosing between Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG +0.57%) and e.l.f. Beauty (ELF -3.33%) face a classic choice between steady restaurant growth and a high-momentum beauty disruptor.

Chipotle relies on its reputation for fresh ingredients and digital convenience to drive volume, while e.l.f. Beauty uses a multi-brand strategy and mass-market retail partnerships to reach younger, value-conscious consumers. Both companies are scaling rapidly while navigating different economic pressures.

Chipotle operates a massive network of company-owned restaurants focused on high-quality ingredients and efficient service across several countries. The company has successfully leaned into digital sales, which accounted for nearly 36.7% of food and beverage revenue in its latest annual report. While expanding its physical footprint, it also relies on third-party delivery services, showing a strong presence among retail stocks in the dining category.

In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached nearly $11.9 billion, representing growth of roughly 5.4% compared with the prior fiscal year. The net margin, which is the percentage of revenue remaining as profit after all costs, was approximately 12.9%. This resulted in a net income of close to $1.5 billion, demonstrating the company's ability to maintain consistent profitability despite rising commodity prices.

e.l.f. Beauty provides cosmetics through an omni-channel strategy that blends e-commerce with major retail partnerships. The company maintains a small number of critical relationships with Target (TGT -3.16%), Walmart (WMT -1.12%), Amazon (AMZN -2.19%), and Sephora, which together represent a significant portion of its sales. Its multi-brand approach, including the recently acquired rhode, allows it to target more of the beauty market.

In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $1.6 billion, a significant increase of approximately 24.6% over the previous year. However, the net margin was roughly 1.6%, leading to a net income of about $26.3 million for the period. This lower profitability relative to previous years reflects the costs associated with integrating new brands and expanding its global footprint.

Chipotle Mexican Grill faces significant risks regarding food safety, as any incident of food-borne illness could severely damage its brand reputation. The company operates in a highly competitive industry and must constantly balance price and quality to retain customers. Furthermore, it deals with supply chain dependencies and complex labor regulations, including potential unionization efforts and scheduling laws that could increase operating costs.

e.l.f. Beauty faces intense competition from established giants like Coty (COTY +12.68%) and L'Oréal (LRLCF +1.40%), which could lead to a loss of valuable retail shelf space. The company relies heavily on a supply chain based in China, making it vulnerable to trade policies, tariffs, and logistics disruptions. Integration risks also persist with its acquisition of rhode, which depends heavily on the continued involvement and public image of key personnel.

Chipotle carries a lower earnings multiple but a similar sales-based valuation compared to the faster-growing beauty brand.

Inflation is still stubborn, interest rate hikes are on the table for the foreseeable future, fears over an artificial intelligence bubble are growing, and there are plenty of other potential unknowns that could affect the markets in 2027. That's why, between the two companies, I would rather own the one generating more net income, as that doesn't fully shield a company from downturns but can offer a safety net during volatile times. With $1.5 billion in net income in 2025 compared to e.l.f.'s $26.3 million for fiscal year 2026, Chipotle easily wins that battle.

That said, beyond its ability to generate profits, I also like that it has revenue growth opportunities. Chipotle opened its 4,000th store in 2025, with a long-term goal of operating 7,000 locations across North America. And in the third quarter of 2026 alone, it opened 84 company-owned restaurants. It's also seeing success by leaning into more digital ordering, with digital sales accounting for 38.8% of total food and beverage revenue for the third quarter. In comparison, that percentage was 36.7% in the prior-year period.

For e.l.f., there are also sales growth opportunities, as only 25% of the company's business comes from outside the United States. Still, Chipotle has a larger market it can serve, giving it more sales to convert into profits.

Jack Delaney has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Amazon, Chipotle Mexican Grill, Target, and Walmart. The Motley Fool recommends e.l.f. Beauty and recommends the following options: short December 2026 $38 calls on Chipotle Mexican Grill. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3069. Here's what the Democratic election rout could mean for the U.S. economy

The Democratic midterm election sweep could result in changes in economic policies related to trade, spending priorities and artificial intelligence. But the biggest forces shaping the economy aren't going to change just because the party in power did.

Affordability pressures, heavy levels of government spending and growth that is dependent on the artificial intelligence tail wind are likely to persist, economists say. And all of those factors pose risks to the economy.

"It's in a very kind of fragile place, and I don't know that it would take a lot to push the economy off the rails, and recession becomes a much greater risk," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "That isn't the case at the moment, but I don't think that's gone away."

Zandi said he had been worried before the election that the economy was under threat from inflation, an underwhelming labor market and geopolitical dangers, and remains concerned now.

Democrats romped to upset wins in not only House and Senate races but also governor and other state races. But economic and foreign policy is largely set in the executive branch, and President Donald Trump remains far apart from his Democratic adversaries, though he said Wednesday he anticipates working with them.

"I don't expect any change in economic policy. The Iran war, the tariffs and trade policy, the heavy-handed immigration policy, all are done under executive order. They're not legislatively driven," Zandi said.

"The president thought they were good policies before the election. I don't know why he'd change his mind after the election," Zandi added. "So I think they will continue to be policies that restrain growth and add to inflationary pressures and interest rates."

Zandi sees the AI hyperscaler buildout as a key to economic growth, but also a source of potential peril.

"The risks are decidedly to the downside because the growth is so dependent on AI, and the AI growth effects are so dependent on the equity market, and the equity market is so dependent on the valuations," he said. "It just feels like kind of a very fragile place, and the labor market is not well functioning."

Local opposition to data centers was a fairly significant issue in the election, particularly for Democrats, according to CNBC polling, so that could be a further economic headwind, though the issue ranked below cost of living, corruption and several others.

The election happened amid a dichotomy in economic views.

Top-line numbers such as gross domestic product, consumer spending and the unemployment rate tell the story of an economy growing briskly while consumers spend and most Americans who want jobs are at work. GDP accelerated at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter while consumer spending grew 3.8%. The unemployment rate is at 4.2% while layoffs are around their lowest level since 1969.

However, rising prices have overshadowed those otherwise solid metrics.

The inflation rate in September as judged by the consumer price index was 3.7% — up sharply from 2.3% in April 2025 when Trump announced an aggressive round of so-called reciprocal tariffs against U.S. trading partners. The Iran war has only aggravated those conditions. The CPI was at just 2.4% when the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran in late February, a war that has caused gas prices to soar.

And wages aren't keeping up with rising costs. Wage growth when adjusted for inflation has turned negative, down 0.7% from a year ago in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

One area where the two sides of the political divide could come together is tariffs.

Congressional Democrats haven't been reflexively opposed to tariff efforts aimed at leveling the playing field. But the Trump tariffs have been criticized for their sweeping nature.

Gary Cohn, who served as director of the National Economic Council during Trump's first term, said Wednesday that he sees room for movement on trade issues.

"There's become a much more universal view on tariffs and what they're good for," Cohn said during a CNBC interview. "Protecting U.S. workers and protecting manufacturing, protecting jobs in the United States, specifically from China, more than anything, is good and has been good policy."

While Cohn noted that "shutting down the borders between Canada and Mexico and the United States has probably not been so good for policy," he thinks "there's a compromise that could be reached where we actually have tariffs put through the legislative system and they become law. They wouldn't become executive orders that can be rescinded the minute the next president walks off the podium."

Democrats would also likely look to roll back spending cuts to SNAP food stamp benefits and Medicaid that were approved by the Republican-controlled Congress under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Morgan Stanley analysts said in a client note. But other policies that Democrats oppose would be harder to reverse.

"We think policy uncertainty since the beginning of President Trump's second term has been tied to executive, not legislative, action," the firm said. "Policies on tariffs, geopolitics, trade ... deregulation, and export controls are all likely to persist, meaning we should expect a certain level of policy uncertainty to continue."

High levels of government debt and budget deficits also are likely to remain.

The national debt currently stands at $40.5 trillion, up more than $4 trillion since Trump took office in January 2025. Net interest on the debt totaled $1.05 trillion in fiscal 2026, higher than spending on any other category except Social Security and Medicare.

The U.S. ended the year with a deficit just shy of $2 trillion, or about 6.1% of GDP. Morgan Stanley expects that level to persist even with some Democratic officials preaching fiscal discipline.

While there are concerns that the change in power could result in standoffs over the debt ceiling, "Democrats are likely to leverage [an impasse] to win policy concessions," Jan Hatzius, chief economist at Goldman Sachs, said in a note.

"It is not yet clear what Democrats will seek in return, but limiting the war with Iran, tariff rollbacks, the reversal of spending cuts, and expanded health benefits appear to be high on the list of priorities," he said.

Despite the various headwinds and political uncertainty, most of Wall Street expects the growth in the economy to continue — if not without hiccups and lingering issues over the cost of living.

"My sense is that the economic expansion will continue to roll on, featuring above trend growth near 2½ percent," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM.

Brusuelas also sees the opportunity to "reset" the trade agreement between the U.S., Mexico and Canada after a year and a half of tension from the Trump tariffs and reprisals.

"We only have a 15% probability of recession over the next 12 months," he said. "The outcome of the election was immaterial to that estimate."

#3067. Wall Street's fear gauge surges the most since April. Why traders think it should be even higher

Whether it's a referendum on the midterms or just a continuation of a bear market in semiconductors that dates back to the group's peak in June, one thing's clear from the options action Thursday: few traders saw this coming.

That's evident in the surge in Cboe Volatility index (VIX), which jumped as much as 5.7 points to above 28 about 90 minutes after the opening bell on Thursday. It's the highest reading on VIX since March 31, the day after the S&P 500 bottomed after selling off as tensions between Iran, Israel and the U.S. reached fever pitch.

From its intraday low to high Thursday, VIX moved more than 11 points, the biggest one-day move since April 9. Yet with the S&P 500 down 3%, there's an argument to be made that volatility should be higher. Traders use a rule of thumb that 16 points for the VIX equate to a 1% move in the index.

The S&P 500 was headed for its worst decline since April 2025.

"My data says to de-risk, but my gut says this is a blowout that could create a dip-buying opportunity" said Noel Smith, "I do not see macro stuff causing this, like oil or rates. Those things are relatively unchanged. The tape looks like a liquidation and that's exactly what it is according to what I'm hearing with regards to a hedge fund."

Looking at Wednesday's response to the selloff in semiconductors adds a wrinkle for traders that pointed to a too-calm VIX despite Wednesday's tech-stock wreck. With the VanEck Semiconductor ETF down 3%, it was the first day in market history that the VIX concurrently fell more than 4 points, according to data from the X account "OddStats." As of midday, nearly 800,000 calls traded on the VIX, 3.5 times higher than 30-day average, according to Cboe data.

#3066. Oracle vs. Alphabet: Which Is the Better AI Cloud Stock to Own for the Next 5 Years?

Both companies are in the middle of an AI spending spree, but Alphabet's prominent position in cloud computing gives it the edge.

There's a growing list of technology companies investing heavily in artificial intelligence (AI) cloud computing as demand for compute capacity accelerates. Bank of America estimates that data center infrastructure spending will more than double to $2.1 trillion by 2028.

But not every company that's spending money now on AI cloud computing will have substantial sales and earnings to show for it later.

Alphabet (GOOGL -2.20%) (GOOG -1.93%) and Oracle (ORCL -6.93%) are two prominent cloud companies ramping up their AI investments right now. Still, while Alphabet's cloud sales are accelerating due to its spending, Oracle's debt is worrying shareholders.

Investors wondering which is the better AI cloud stock to own over the next five years need only look at Google Cloud's third-quarter sales doubling for their answer. Here's why Alphabet is the safer long-term bet.

Alphabet stock fell hard recently amid investor concerns about its high capital expenditures, which are expected to reach up to $205 billion this year. The spending has resulted in $9.1 billion in negative free cash flow, worrying many Alphabet shareholders.

But investors seemed to misunderstand two factors: First, $5.1 billion of the negative free cash flow was from a one-time fee to the European Commission, making the decline not as bad as it first appears. The second is that Alphabet's AI spending already appears to be paying off amid rising Google Cloud sales.

Consider that Google Cloud sales more than doubled in the third quarter (which ended Sept. 30) to $30.7 billion. That's an exceptionally high growth rate and shows why the company's capex is rising so quickly.

Rising demand for computing capacity is encouraging Alphabet to ramp up spending, and as expensive as it is, demand appears to continue outpacing capacity. The company said Google Cloud has a $561 billion cloud backlog, which it estimates will convert to sales over the next 24 months.

Negative free cash flow isn't great to see, I'll admit. But the company can always pull back spending once it has enough compute capacity. And when it does, its soaring cloud sales will likely help bring the company's free cash flow back into positive territory -- especially considering that Google Cloud's operating income recently tripled to $11 billion and operating margins have increased to 36%.

Oracle is also investing heavily in data center infrastructure, with management saying that capital expenditures will total up to $95 billion this year. That's up from $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026.

Investors have been skeptical about Oracle's accelerating spending, and they really haven't liked how the company is paying for it by taking on debt. To ease concerns, leadership recently said it would limit its capital raises through fiscal 2030 to an additional $20 billion (on top of an additional $20 billion raised recently).

While that temporarily eased investor fears, they came roaring back just days later when Oracle announced it would raise all of that $20 billion immediately rather than over the next few years. Oracle has about $169 billion in total debt, which has spooked investors and resulted in Oracle's stock falling 50% over the past year.

It may not be all bad news for Oracle investors, though, as management says free cash flow could be $30 billion or more in fiscal 2029 -- a stark contrast to its negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026.

If you feel comfortable with some additional risk, Oracle stock could be a good investment as the company's spending slows and free cash flow rebounds over the next couple of years.

But I think Alphabet looks like the better AI cloud stock over the next five years. It's already the third-largest cloud player and is poised to generate significant sales from its massive Google Cloud backlog.

#3061. Cloudflare Sales Up 39%, Gross Margin Falls: Rapid Earnings Reaction

Cloudflare is growing quickly, and the release shows where the cost of that growth landed. We look at margins, cash flow, and what the GAAP numbers add.

Cloudflare (NET -8.28%) grew third-quarter revenue 39% to $782.5 million. Shares jumped about 15% in after-hours trading. Growth is strong, and each new dollar of sales now leaves less behind. Gross margin fell about 3 points, and free cash flow margin slipped to 10% from 13%.

Cost of revenue grew 54%, far faster than sales, which alone explains the lower gross margin. The release does not say why. Cloudflare runs its own global network, so added capacity hits cost of revenue and capital spending before the sales that fill it.

Non-GAAP operating margin improved, but GAAP shows a wider loss. The gap is mostly stock-based pay and related payroll taxes, which rose 45%, faster than revenue.

#3060. Trump's energy deals are about to face a wave of investigations by Democrats

President Donald Trump is expected to face a wave of investigations when Democrats take control of Congress in January. His sweeping deal-making in the energy sector is likely to become a central focus.

Democrats have pressed the White House for months on the legality of its intervention in Venezuela's oil sector and its cancellation of renewable energy projects funded by the Biden administration. They have raised conflict of interest concerns over numerous deals in the minerals sector.

But, until now, the opposition party could do little more than send strongly worded letters to administration officials. When the next Congress convenes in January, the Democrats will wield the subpoena power that comes with committee control, giving them the authority to compel testimony and the disclosure of documents.

The House Energy and Commerce Committee in the next Congress intends to pursue an aggressive oversight agenda to root out corruption, Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who will likely chair the panel, said in a statement.

With comfortable majorities in the House and Senate, Democrats will likely pass a war powers resolution that demands an end to the conflict, which has hiked fuel prices in the U.S. and around the world.

Crude oil prices sold off sharply Wednesday as the market expected the election defeat to push Trump to cut a deal with Iran. Vice President JD Vance blamed the Republican loss directly on the war, raising questions about whether there is support inside the administration to continue the conflict.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who will likely take over the House speaker's gavel in January, said Wednesday that Democrats will "end this reckless and costly war of choice that has skyrocketed gas prices all across the country."

The new Congress will try to rein in the administration by passing legislation to stop the conflict, said Rep. Ted Lieu, vice chairman of the Democratic caucus. Jeffries has said Democrats will pass a war powers resolution, though Trump will almost certainly wield his veto. It is unclear whether Democrats will try to restrict funding for the war as well.

Nevertheless, tumbling crude prices could push gasoline below $4 per gallon in the next week and diesel under $6 by Thanksgiving, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, in a social media post Wednesday.

But the odds still favor military escalation in the Middle East, warned Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush.

"Iran is hardened in its uncompromising position," McNally said. "Trump, having now paid a huge price for his determination to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, is unlikely to let go of this legacy goal and walk away."

Democratic lawmakers have pressed the Trump administration for months to provide Congress with an accounting of how Venezuela's oil revenues have been spent — to no avail.

Washington seized control of Venezuela's oil exports in January after ousting former President Nicolás Maduro in a military raid. The Pentagon took a stake in an obscure oil company, North American Blue Energy Partners, or NABEP, that is supposed to develop Venezuelan oil reserves. The deal supposedly gives the U.S. control over 65 billion barrels of oil.

Democratic House members warned the oil industry in January that entering into an agreement with the U.S. on Venezuelan oil could expose the industry to "legal risk, including civil liability from creditors who hold nearly $200 billion worth of debt to Venezuela and their various state-owned entities."

Democratic senators subsequently sent a letter in September to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Energy Secretary Chris Wright questioning the legal basis for the U.S. government's deal with NABEP.

Energy analysts warned when the NABEP deal was announced in August that it might not survive if Democrats take power in Washington.

Democrats have also raised conflict of interest concerns over the Trump administration's series of deals in the critical minerals sector.

The White House has justified the deals, often involving government equity stakes in private companies, as necessary to support a segment of the mining industry that's critical to U.S. national security and that has been undercut by competitors in China.

But Democratic senators have pointed to the involvement of Cantor Fitzgerald in a number of those deals as cause for concern. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ran Cantor before joining the Trump administration. He personally divested from Cantor after joining the Cabinet and turned over control to his sons.

The Democratic senators demanded in a July letter that the federal government preserve any records related to deals involving 14 companies.

For his part, the Commerce secretary dismissed the allegations. "If the Democrats send me letters, I will respond to the letters but they don't matter, since when you do nothing wrong, you don't worry about it and you don't care," Lutnick told CNBC in a September interview."You just answer their silly questions and you move on," Lutnick said. "This is a waste of time trying to create something that doesn't exist."

Others are less cavalier. USA Rare Earth, one of the companies named in the senators' letter, has warned investors that its deal making the U.S. government one of its stockholders has few precedents.

As a consequence, the company could be subject to litigation, political scrutiny and a change in federal priorities, it said in a March filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The Trump administration has favored fossil fuels and waged a relentless campaign against renewable energy, particularly wind power, since taking office.

Democrats are unlikely to restore tax credits phased out by Trump's big tax bill due to the president's veto power. But they are certain to press the administration on the nearly $8 billion of energy projects it has canceled in states that supported Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright has told Congress that the projects were not canceled based on political considerations. Several House Democrats have accused Wright of giving false testimony, an allegation the Energy Department has denied.

Democrats are also scrutinizing the administration's efforts to kill offshore wind power in the U.S. The Interior Department has tried to buy out leases for several such projects, for example, paying TotalEnergies nearly $1 billion to cancel an offshore wind project and stop investing in any similar projects in the U.S. in the future. Total agreed to invest in natural gas instead.

Reps. Jared Huffman and Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrats on the natural resources and judiciary committees, respectively, called the TotalEnergies deal unlawful and launched an investigation in April.

#3055. A 'demand decade' ahead for energy? BP, Baker Hughes CEOs weigh the investment outlook

Rising energy demand is creating new investment opportunities even as geopolitical risks and uncertain oil prices challenge the industry.

Baker Hughes CEO Lorenzo Simonelli is optimistic about the longer-term outlook, pointing to AI, population growth and developing nations as factors supporting continued energy demand growth.

"I think we have a 'demand decade' ahead of us," Simonelli told CNBC's Dan Murphy on "Access Middle East" at the ADIPEC energy conference in Abu Dhabi. "We're looking at very much seeing capital investments improve and increase over time," as growing consumption will require additional infrastructure to support demand.

However, turning that demand into profitability may be a challenge.

Markus Krebber, CEO of German energy company RWE, said AI and electrification were driving electricity demand, but geopolitical tensions, supply chain pressures and higher interest rates were complicating investment decisions.

"You have huge investment opportunity, but on the other hand, a very challenging investment environment," Krebber said during a separate ADIPEC discussion. On planned expansions in computing capacity and the power needed to support them, he said "it's going to come, but it probably comes slow."

The wide range of global energy demand forecasts is an important consideration in investment decisions, given that new oil and gas projects can take years to develop and remain in production for decades, BP CEO Meg O'Neill said at ADIPEC.

She also highlighted the uncertainty surrounding oil prices, saying that "we need to plan our business for a lower-price environment."

Industry activity is expected to rise by a low-single-digit percentage in 2027, according to Simonelli. The Middle East conflict has highlighted the need for more resilient energy infrastructure, including additional storage and pipelines, he said.

"If you look at the energy system, though, what it really means is it's going to have to be more resilient," Simonelli said. "That means more storage. It means more pipelines. It means eliminating choke points that exist today."

Schneider Electric CEO Olivier Blum noted that some projects in the Persian Gulf have slowed because of the Middle East conflict. However, "in the mid-term, I would say the opportunity for more infrastructure has even increased," he told CNBC.

The investment equation also depends on the supply outlook, of course.

Oil markets could face oversupply in 2027 and 2028, Richard Bronze, co-founder and head of geopolitics at energy consultancy Energy Aspects, told CNBC in a separate interview.

Supply-demand forecasts, including those from Energy Aspects, "project an oversupplied market 2027, 2028 — if we get Middle Eastern flows back to normal," Bronze said.

#3054. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3048. Inside India newsletter: India weighs a tax cut to win over foreign investors. Will it work?

Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.

Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.

Once a favorite emerging market for foreign investors, Indian equities have been losing their charm. Foreign holdings of Indian stocks are currently at an all-time low of 14%. Now a tax cut, which puts India on par with several Asian markets, is being proposed to win back these investors.

This week, I spoke with experts to find out whether a tax cut alone can restore the Indian stock market's appeal to foreign investors.

Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.

The clamor for removing tax on long-term capital gains, or LTCG, on foreign portfolio investors is rising in India as the country's equity markets witness record capital outflows.

On Monday, Reuters reported that India's capital market regulator has urged the government to scrap the LTCG tax for foreign investors.

One of India's oldest and most prominent industry bodies, PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, last week asked the government appealing to abolish the tax.

It argued that the capital gains tax was increased in 2024 at a time when the stock market was "near record highs" and as the market conditions have now changed, the government needs to review it.

The country's Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Monday acknowledged the exit of foreign capital outflows and added she would consider the calls for reviewing LTCG tax, as per local media reports.

These demands come at a time when foreign investors' appetite for Indian equities has sharply declined. As per a Nomura report on Monday, foreign holdings in Indian stocks are at an all-time low of 14%.

Experts agree that the removal of the tax cut would improve foreign investors' sentiment by putting India's tax regime on par with other emerging markets. But the tax cut alone may not be enough to bring back foreign investors in droves, they said.

"A tax cut helps at the margin, but allocators tend to buy expected returns, not tax breaks," said Amit Bhartia, portfolio manager at Singapore-based Delorean Partners. He added that foreign investors have exited India as earnings growth became less predictable, while risks shot up.

Bhartia highlighted that foreign investors put in about 570 billion rupees ($6 billion) into Indian equities in September of 2024, and a month later pulled out 940 billion rupees to chase cheaper Chinese stocks. "The tax rate didn't change between those two months. The perceived relative return did," Bhartia explained.

Until the record exit in March this year, the outflows in October 2024 were the highest in a month.

Multiple risks are weighing down Indian markets right now, including strained ties with the U.S., higher energy prices, a depreciating currency and uncertainty over the impact of artificial intelligence.

A possible LTCG cut for foreign investors, a drop in global bond yields and expectations of the rupee holding up on central bank intervention would lend support to the Indian markets, Nomura said in its report.

However, it added that from a longer-term perspective, concerns around geopolitical and technological uncertainty persist, "weighing on long-term growth expectations."

India was the world's third worst-performing market after Indonesia and Turkey between January and October this year, the report showed. India's benchmark Nifty 50 as lost nearly 9% so far this year.

Foreign investors, who just three years ago celebrated India as the best-performing emerging market, have soured over the last two years, cashing out net $18.9 billion in 2025 and more than $30 billion so far this year.

India has "to fight for capital in a competition it could once afford to take for granted," global brokerage Bernstein said in a report on Monday. It argued that multiple "catalysts," including a tax cut and easing of tensions in the Middle East, are needed to reverse capital outflows from India.

"India's valuations remain expensive, while earnings growth has been disappointing," the report said.

As per the data shared in the report, India is trading at a rolling 12-month forward price-to-earnings of 18.6 times, higher than Taiwan's 16.8 times and Korea's 3.9 times. Both these markets have been outperformers in the emerging countries, propped up by strong artificial intelligence names.

On the earnings growth front, while emerging markets on average are expected to deliver a 45% improvement, India's forecast is much slower at 11%, as per Bernstein.

The tax cut alone will not "trigger a major reallocation into Indian equities as the fundamental trade-off facing foreign investors remains unchanged," Hanna Luchnikava-Schorsch, head of Asia-Pacific economics at S&P Global Market Intelligence, told CNBC.

As cracks emerge in the global AI rally, data from LSEG shows Indian benchmark indexes have outperformed global peers over the past month, as some investors see the Indian market as a hedge against AI. Foreign capital flows at the start of this month have been positive. But will they sustain?

India has a strong structural growth story, but investors still need earnings growth to justify the valuation premium, Luchnikava-Schorsch said.

#3042. Inside the chip talent war: Trade secrets and rising Chinese rivals

A former Samsung Electronics employee who later joined Chinese memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, was reportedly sentenced by the Seoul High Court on Oct. 22 to five years in prison for leaking Samsung's technology.

The sentence was reduced from seven years at his first trial in April. The former employee had joined CXMT in 2016.

The case highlights an intensifying battle over semiconductor know-how as Chinese chipmakers narrow the gap with established rivals, putting the race for top engineering talent increasingly at odds with efforts to protect trade secrets.

In 2023, a South Korean court granted Samsung's request to block a former DRAM researcher from joining U.S. rival Micron. It ruled that the two-year non-compete was not excessive and was necessary to protect Samsung's technology and business information, JoongAng Ilbo reported.

A decade ago, Chinese memory chipmakers were not Samsung's biggest concern when it came to losing experienced engineers.

Instead, the South Korean company was more focused on employees leaving for established rivals such as SK Hynix and Micron, according to a former employee who asked not to be identified because the information was private.

Samsung has been monitoring where certain departing employees went — to signal to remaining staff that moving to competitors would be difficult — according to a former employee.

The company also used non-compete agreements restricting employees from joining rivals for two years, as part of their employment contracts, with senior employees holding valuable technical expertise likely facing closer scrutiny.

But Samsung's concern extended beyond individual departures.

"It wasn't just about one employee leaving. The company wanted to send a message to those who stayed that moving to a competitor wouldn't be easy," the former employee said.

Meanwhile, Chinese semiconductor companies have sought to close the technology gap by recruiting experienced overseas engineers with high salaries, stock options, housing and family support, according to Jeongku Choi, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research.

Their expertise has helped Chinese chipmakers overcome technical bottlenecks, particularly as U.S. export restrictions have limited China's access to advanced chipmaking equipment, Choi said.

Once viewed as unlikely to catch up with established players, Chinese manufacturers are now seen as "meaningful competitors," she added.

Counterpoint's Memory Tracker for the second quarter of 2026 projected CXMT's share of global DRAM revenue would reach 10%.

Established chipmakers are strengthening legal protections and internal security measures while adjusting compensation packages to retain key engineers, according to Choi.

South Korea has also designated certain semiconductor manufacturing technologies as "National Core Technologies," raising the penalties for unauthorized leaks of those technologies, Choi said.

The legal battle could intensify as Chinese memory companies expand beyond their home market.

"I believe that this management of trade secrets will expand its scope even further to IP and legal areas once Chinese memory companies move beyond the Chinese market and begin to expand their exports," Choi said.

The growing competition is putting greater focus on how semiconductor companies protect the knowledge accumulated by engineers working on complex manufacturing processes.

In Taiwan, home to the world's largest contract chipmaker TSMC, protections for trade secrets have evolved alongside the semiconductor industry’s growing strategic importance.

Jamie J. Yang, a partner specializing in antitrust and intellectual property at Innovatus Law, said Taiwan limits post-employment non-compete agreements to two years and requires employers to compensate former employees at least half their average monthly salary during the restricted period.

Yang added that the complexity of semiconductor manufacturing makes it difficult for any single engineer to possess enough knowledge to replicate an entire production line elsewhere.

"There is just very little chance that one person ... will know enough to replicate that line in any of the other companies," Yang said.

Moves by engineers between rival semiconductor companies could increase modestly as competition for top talent intensifies, while trade secret litigation is also likely to rise as firms seek to protect their technological edge, she added.

In Singapore, Zechariah Chan, a partner at law firm Lee & Lee, said protecting trade secrets can be particularly difficult in the semiconductor industry, where proprietary knowledge often involves intangible manufacturing techniques and methods.

Proving that a competitor has used proprietary manufacturing techniques can also be difficult, as outsiders generally see only the final product, according to Chan.

"There is no bright line between an engineer's expertise and proprietary information," he said. General skills and knowledge stay with the engineer, while trade secrets remain with the company.

In Singapore, non-compete clauses are enforceable only if they protect legitimate business interests and are reasonable in scope, geographical area and duration.

In Hong Kong, courts generally take a restrictive approach to non-compete clauses, enforcing them only when they protect legitimate business interests and go no further than necessary, according to Jezamine Fewins, head of litigation at Lewis Silkin in Hong Kong.

Courts are more willing to protect trade secrets through court injunctions, Fewins said.

"The difficulty is that often the trade secret is carried in the employee's head," she added. Information is more likely to qualify as a trade secret if its disclosure to a competitor could cause significant harm to the former employer and the company has taken steps to restrict access.

For chipmakers, Fewins said the key is to clearly define what constitutes a trade secret, make employees aware of that information and put safeguards in place to limit access.

Samsung and CXMT did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.

#3041. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

Carmelo Anthony and La La Anthony at the Houston Cougars-Syracuse Orange game during the Players Era Basketball Championship at MGM Grand Garden Arena on November 24, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. Getty Images

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

#3023. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.
